title_en: Microsoft's president says AI is less regulated than a carton of milk
title_fa: Microsoft's president says AI is less regulated than a carton of milk
excerpt_en: Milk can't hack companies and governments like AI definitely can, but it's still subject to more regulation.
excerpt_fa: Milk can't hack companies and governments like AI definitely can, but it's still subject to more regulation.
content_en:
Microsoft's president says AI is less regulated than a carton of milk
Brad Smith said the lack of US action gives the UK a unique opening to lead in terms of regulating AI.
Milk can't hack companies and governments like AI definitely can, but it's still subject to more regulation, Microsoft president Brad Smith told ITV on Friday. "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI," Smith said in the interview. "Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."
Major US AI giants like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google's DeepMind have spoken in favor of an AI development slowdown. However, US President Donald Trump has said that, if anything, the US AI industry needs to accelerate to stay ahead of China.
Rather than government, Trump would prefer that AI companies regulate themselves. At his so-called Super Intelligence summit, AI bosses including Google Sundar Pichai, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Elon Musk and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang signed a pact with several key tenets. Those include implementing self-regulation, safeguards to keep pioneer models from going rogue and using "independent auditors" to assess models.
Critics were unimpressed, though, with one telling the BBC that it allows firms to "define what counts as safety" and another saying that "the accord should be ignored for the distraction it is."
Microsoft's Smith thinks the lack of US action gives the UK a unique opening to lead in terms of regulating AI. "In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels — that's a strength," he said. "I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country. [W]hen you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk, I would say: the moment has arrived."

title_en: The pros and cons of importing foreign phones to the US
title_fa: The pros and cons of importing foreign phones to the US
excerpt_en: Foreign phones can bring new features not often seen in the US, but you need to make sure they're compatible with your carrier.
excerpt_fa: Foreign phones can bring new features not often seen in the US, but you need to make sure they're compatible with your carrier.
content_en:
The pros and cons of importing foreign phones to the US
There's a lot to consider before buying a new phone from abroad.
There are plenty of smartphone options to choose from in the US, from the iPhone to the Pixel. But there are also really interesting phones you'll never find in an American store. Xiaomi's foldables like the Mix Fold, Honor's Magic series and OPPO's Find X phones are a few examples that offer unique designs or features not generally seen in the US.
While phones like these are harder to find in the country, it's possible to import them, but bringing a phone from abroad has its downsides. You may have problems using your phone with local carriers or getting warranty coverage, among other trouble. If you're considering an imported phone, always check a few points first.
What you should know before buying a phone from another country
Buying an imported phone has become a lot easier in recent years. Most smartphones are now designed to work globally on most cellular bands. Still, some phones may not work with those used by your US carrier. Start by checking whether the phone you're considering is compatible with your carrier's frequency bands. Buying the wrong version could leave you stuck on the LTE network with no 5G support.
Carrier-specific features can cause issues too. Features like Wi-Fi calling, VoLTE and visual voicemail usually require certification for each device. So even if your imported phone works fine on your carrier's 5G network, it might not be able to access all these features in the US. Network requirements may also change, so a model that works fine today may run into problems in the future. It's worth checking forums like Reddit to see what people who've bought the phone you want have to say.
Then there are software updates; the rollout of Android updates may be tied to carriers or regions. Also, some Chinese phones are not compatible with Google Play Services, which are a core part of the Android experience most people expect. You may have to install updates manually, and the software might include Chinese apps and services that aren't relevant to you (or readable).
Additionally, getting warranty service in the US for these phones may not be easy. Some of these brands have no official representation in the country, which also means no customer support. Dealing with problems like a dead battery or a cracked screen may require taking your phone to a third-party repair shop with no official authorization from the manufacturer.
The benefits of importing a smartphone
If you're okay with all these hassles, importing a phone from abroad can be a lot of fun and open you up to new hardware that isn't available in the US. There are a lot of Chinese companies putting out exciting products, like three-screen foldables, flagships with DSLR-quality cameras and devices with massive batteries. The Xiaomi 18 Fold is a new foldable phone that looks similar to the iPhone Duo, but it has a bigger battery and better cameras. It also costs less (the equivalent of about $1,640 currently), but you'll need to buy it abroad if you want to use it in the US.
For those who want the latest releases, importing a phone often gives you the chance to get it before the official US launch. Also, many international models still support two physical SIM cards — a feature that most phones sold in the US have already ditched in favor of eSIM. If you don't mind the potential drawbacks, it can be a rewarding experience. But if it's important that you have official support nearby and know all features will work properly on your network, it's easier to buy a phone that's officially supported in your country.

title_en: OpenAI Dot vs. Meta Muse: How do these AI agents compare?
title_fa: OpenAI Dot vs. Meta Muse: How do these AI agents compare?
excerpt_en: Meta and OpenAI's new AI agents are in direct competition. Here's what each can do, what they cost and who has access.
excerpt_fa: Meta and OpenAI's new AI agents are in direct competition. Here's what each can do, what they cost and who has access.
content_en:
OpenAI Dot vs. Meta Muse: How do these AI agents compare?
Both agents can keep working after you leave, but they differ considerably on price, permissions and where they can work.
Meta and OpenAI now have AI agents that are meant to do more than just wait for the next prompt. Meta released Muse on September 8, followed by OpenAI's new always-on agents in ChatGPT three weeks later. Both can continue to work after you leave, run their own cloud computers and connect to outside services.
The promise is enticing: Provide an AI with a task and then stop checking on it every five minutes. Muse can go shopping, complete forms, make travel plans, send emails and monitor things such as prices. Dots can manage ongoing research, work across connected applications and perform recurring tasks, and OpenAI is closely integrating them with ChatGPT, Work and Codex.
Dots and Muse can do similar jobs, but the experience is different
Muse runs on a dedicated Secure VM with its own browser and is designed to feel a lot like messaging another person. It can be used via Muse's apps, the web or WhatsApp, and then linked with services like email and your calendar when you're ready to make it more powerful. In Engadget's hands-on, Muse turned saved Instagram and Facebook posts into organized recipe and restaurant collections.
Dot lives within ChatGPT and is powered by GPT-6 Astra. Each one has its own cloud computer, can utilize connected plugins, remembers relevant context and can keep working on scheduled or recurring jobs. Users can also grant a Dot access to their local computer to retrieve files or browse the internet, and OpenAI plans to enable users to manage multiple Dots simultaneously.
That's where the sci-fi sheen fades a bit, since these agents still need supervision. Meta states that Muse asks for permission before taking sensitive actions like sending an email or making a purchase, and OpenAI employs permissions, Custom Rules and Auto-review to manage what Dots can do, with both companies cautioning that their agents can make mistakes. Even browser access has limits: Amazon has already blocked Muse from shopping on its site.
Muse is much cheaper to try, but privacy controls matter on both
The most obvious difference is price. The free tier of Muse has a usage cap, and the Power and Maximum tiers are $20 and $100 per month, respectively. At present, individual users must pay a much higher subscription fee to use Dots, with the lowest available option being Pro 100 for $100 per month. A Business Premium seat costs $100 per user per month (billed annually) or $125 per user per month (billed monthly).
The subscription isn't the only thing, of course. The more accounts you link, the more capable the agent becomes, but that can mean access to your email, calendar, files and browser sessions (which is not something most people would give away lightly). Meta states that conversations and data within its VM aren't shared with its advertising systems, and that users can choose not to have the interactions used to enhance Meta's AI models. Engadget found the model-improvement setting enabled by default, along with a default permission option that prompts for only some actions.
OpenAI states that activity from personal-plan Dots may be used to improve its models, depending on the user's ChatGPT setting, while Business and Enterprise data is not used for training by default. Proactive Dot research is read-only until a subsequent action passes its normal permission checks.
Availability is another complication. Dots are rolling out to eligible Pro users outside the European Economic Area (EEA), Switzerland and the UK, while Dots are available to Business Premium users across supported ChatGPT regions, and Enterprise access is still in beta. OpenAI states that Dot usage won't count toward your usage limits unless the Dot is working within ChatGPT Work or Codex. Muse is currently available in the US and Canada.

title_en: Mbps Vs MB/s: What do these speeds mean?
title_fa: Mbps Vs MB/s: What do these speeds mean?
excerpt_en: Know the difference between bits and bytes.
excerpt_fa: Know the difference between bits and bytes.
content_en:
Mbps Vs MB/s: What do these speeds mean?
Know the difference between bits and bytes.
Its easy to lose yourself in the morass of technical terminologies when shopping for internet providers. For instance, debates over whether you should prioritize internet speed vs. bandwidth or whether you need a Wi-Fi 7 router can easily derail your search if you don't know what to look for. A prevalent and consequential mix up is between Megabits per second (Mbps) and Megabytes per second (MB/s). Although both are measurements of data transfers, confusing them can have major implications.
To understand the two, you first have to grapple with the difference between bits and bytes. Bits are the basic unit of information for computing and measure the binary 1s and 0s of that make up a string of code. Bits per second are commonly used to measure the speed of data transfers, such as internet streaming speeds or download speeds. Bytes, on the other hand, are groups of eight bits – the typical amount to produce a single letter, symbol or number. These metrics are used to describe file sizes or storage space. For instance, you might describe the size of a movie file in terms of bytes. When using bytes per second, you are typically gauging how fast these files can be transferred. Considering both units are too small to meaningfully describe contemporary computing power, the prefix "mega" is added to indicate that each measure one million units. The per-second measures of Mbps and MB/s refer to how quickly a million bits and bytes can move, respectively.
What is each term used for?
Understanding megabit per second rates is critical to gauging the quality of your home internet speed. Typically, download speeds severely outpace upload speeds. The FCC, for instance, lists 100 Mbps as the threshold for broadband internet speed, while the requirement for uploading information is merely 20 Mbps. According to a report by internet speed test company Ookla, the median download and upload speeds for American households in August 2026 was 307 Mbps and 63 Mbps, respectively. These average speeds have skyrocketed over the past decade. In 2015, for instance, the FCC's benchmarks for highspeed internet were four times slower than their current standards. If your internet connection continues to perform middlingly, you can potentially boost your Mbps through a few simple fixes.
Megabytes per second, on the other hand, is typically used to describe the speed of a large data transfer to and from a storage device. For instance, you may use the measure to describe how fast a file can be uploaded to the cloud, or how quickly it can be moved from a hard disk. Using megabytes per second, you can easily quantify how long it will take you to download a video file or transfer a document.
Of course, you may see the two metrics used interchangeably. Luckily, comparing the two metrics is simple: just divide your megabits by eight. For instance, if your internet says that it can upload a file at 100 Mbps, that equates to 12.5 MBps. Conversely, to convert MBps to Mbps simply multiply by 8.

title_en: The reason the Xbox Series S is so much cheaper than the Series X
title_fa: The reason the Xbox Series S is so much cheaper than the Series X
excerpt_en: The Xbox Series X and S have seen the same price hikes as all other gaming hardware, but the Series S still provides a lower cost to entry.
excerpt_fa: The Xbox Series X and S have seen the same price hikes as all other gaming hardware, but the Series S still provides a lower cost to entry.
content_en:
The reason the Xbox Series S is so much cheaper than the Series X
Both consoles have become more expensive since launch, but the Series S is still relatively affordable.
A console nearly six years into its lifecycle would typically have seen a price drop by this point, but that's not the case for the latest Xbox line. On the contrary, the Xbox Series X and S have seen a price increase in recent months. It's not the only system to see these hikes, either. The PlayStation 5's price went up twice within a year and the Nintendo Switch 2 got a heftier price tag in 2026, largely thanks to the ongoing RAMaggedon crisis driving up component prices.
Despite the price hikes, the Series S maintains a price edge over the Series X, starting at $500. That's a stark difference from the Series X's cheapest $750 model, and means the Series S is tied with the Switch 2 for the most affordable modern console. But why is the Series S so much cheaper than the Series X? It all comes down to hardware.
Why the Series X is more expensive
The most obvious difference between these two is that the Series S is a digital-only device that lacks a disc drive. Though there is a model of the Series X that also lacks a disc drive (which knocks $50 off its price), the hardware of the Series X otherwise remains the same. This lock-in to a solely digital landscape is one of the most defining features between the two, which contributes somewhat to its cheaper price tag.
Under the hood, the Series S is also a less impressive piece of hardware then the Series X. The base model of the Series S offers 512GB of storage, with a 1TB model available for $100 more. Meanwhile, the Series X comes with 1TB of space (there was a 2TB Series X model, but Microsoft discontinued it in 2026). Either model can gain more storage with an expansion card that plugs into the back of the console.
The Series X boasts 12 teraflops of processing power and targets 4K resolution, while the Series S has only 4 teraflops and can go up to 1440p in most games. However, both consoles have the capability for 120 fps. On a more technical level, both consoles utilize a custom AMD Zen 2 CPU, but the Series X CPU is clocked higher, giving it an edge in speed. Both also use an AMD RDNA 2 GPU, but the Series X version has 52 CUs (short for compute units, a measurement of processing power) while the Series S has only 20.
Similarly, the Series X has 16GB of RAM, 10GB of which can operate at 560 GB per second and 6GB that can operate at 336 GB/s. Compared to 10GB RAM in the S, with 8GB of it operating at 224 GB/s and 2GB at 56 GB/s, the Series X has much more complex and capable hardware, contributing to its higher price.
Xbox Series X vs. Series S: Which is better for you?
If you're set on getting an Xbox console, which Series is right for you depends on your gaming style. If you aren't someone who has a collection of physical games, or largely plan to play via Game Pass, the Series S's lack of disc drive probably won't bother you. If you prefer to take advantage of disc-based game sales or just hold a game in your hands, the Series X is the way to go.
The Series S is the more compact choice, not just from the space saved by skipping physical games, but because it's about 60 percent smaller than a Series X. It's much easier to slot a Series S into an entertainment center than its larger sibling.
Game resolution and performance will be lower with a Series S, but depending on the games you play and your tolerances, it might not be a big enough difference to matter. If you don't need to see 4K resolution all the time (the S does support 4K upscaling, just not 4K natively), or play many games that aren't graphically intensive, the Series S might be good enough, especially since it can achieve 120 fps in compatible titles. However, if you're a performance purist who wants the very best, you'll want the Series X.
Alternatively, it's worth waiting until Microsoft's Project Helix family of devices comes out if you'd rather not get a console so many years into its lifecycle. These will almost certainly be more expensive than a Series X or S, and we don't know how big the technical advancements will be between this generation and the next. Microsoft plans to start sending alpha Project Helix hardware to developers in 2027, which likely means at least another year after that before we see the final product released. But if you're willing to be patient, consider saving your money for cutting-edge technology.

However, if you're a performance purist who wants the very best, you'll want the Series X.
Alternatively, it's worth waiting until Microsoft's Project Helix family of devices comes out if you'd rather not get a console so many years into its lifecycle. These will almost certainly be more expensive than a Series X or S, and we don't know how big the technical advancements will be between this generation and the next. Microsoft plans to start sending alpha Project Helix hardware to developers in 2027, which likely means at least another year after that before we see the final product released. But if you're willing to be patient, consider saving your money for cutting-edge technology.

title_en: Why Japan said goodbye to traditional flip phones
title_fa: Why Japan said goodbye to traditional flip phones
excerpt_en: Flip phones endured in Japan longer than the US, but the trend is shifting.
excerpt_fa: Flip phones endured in Japan longer than the US, but the trend is shifting.
content_en:
Why Japan said goodbye to traditional flip phones
Flip phones endured in Japan longer than the US, but the trend is shifting.
Chances are you haven't seen a flip phone in the wild for years. The days of the old Motorola RAZR and similar clamshells are long gone. But in Japan, its esoteric tech ecosystem kept them in circulation for decades.
The gara-kei, short for Galapagos keitai, are Japan's curious feature phones with physical keyboards that refused to die in an era of big-screened smartphones. "Galapagos" refers to the isolated islands in the Pacific Ocean, and keitai stands for "portable." For a time, Japanese mobile carriers sold enough of these basic handsets to inspire hybrid garaho phones from brands like Kyocera that paired clamshells with Android and 4G connectivity.
But consumer habits are changing. A Docomo survey in Japan found that smartphones accounted for 90 percent of mobile phone owners in 2021 and 98 percent by 2025. The country's feature phone shipments fell by over 25 percent to under 400,000 units in the first half of fiscal year 2025, according to research firm MM Research Institute.
It's a slow decline poised to accelerate after carrier NTT Docomo ended the country's remaining 3G data service this March. Why, and how, is the venerable gara-kei going extinct?
How did flip phones become so popular in Japan?
Many believe that the gara-kei has strong ties to Japan's culture. It had features well beyond regular flip phones designed for other markets. In addition to durable builds and tactile keyboards, many of these phones could pick up One-Seg TV broadcasts and share contact info via infrared transmitters long before Apple's NameDrop was a thing. They're also stunning to look at, featuring vibrant colors and lanyard holes for exotic keychains.
Most gara-kei offered 3G support for lightweight applications that didn't consume much data. Embedded chips allowed them to pay for trains and groceries, making these phones on cheap contracts integral to living in Japan.
Companies in the US have also attempted to cash in on nostalgia and Gen Z's yearning for flip phones. The upcoming Light Flip is no gara-kei, but it does target users who want a distraction-free flip phone experience. Traditional gara-kei from Kyocera and Sharp are available for purchase on storefronts like eBay, even if most of them lack the right 4G LTE network bands to work with American network carriers.
What's causing the shift away from flip phones in Japan?
Sunsetting i-mode, Docomo's 3G mobile internet, is estimated to affect half a million people and over 400 phone models in Japan, according to The Guardian. It will also impair car navigation systems and vending machines in the country. The announcement rang the death knell for the gara-kei, following au and SoftBank ending 3G service in 2022 and 2024, respectively.
Japan's aging population is another piece of the puzzle. In 2024, 29 percent of its population was aged 65 or above, according to the World Economic Forum, building an economy reliant on senior support. Tens of thousands of "lonely deaths" among the elderly may have reshaped how Japan uses cellular technology. In a bid to boost tech literacy, Japan Today reported that Tokyo handed out 3,000 smartphones to senior citizens in 2021.
While some Gen Z users jumped ship to feature phones in a bid to reclaim their attention spans, many will have to return to their smartphones if they want to remain connected to the internet. Docomo sees the inevitable migration as an opportunity and is promoting its in-store smartphone classrooms that teach people how to handle smartphones.
Lessons on web browsing and gesture controls are accompanied by the risk of gaining an appetite for social-media-powered doomscrolling and growing reliant on these pocket-sized computers. It's the end of an era in Japan for a generation that grew up clicking away on feature phones to stay in touch with the world.

title_en: Study finds many new cars share your data with third-party companies
title_fa: Study finds many new cars share your data with third-party companies
excerpt_en: A study by Northeastern University and Consumer Reports found that automakers are collecting data to allow advertisers to build in-depth profiles on consumers.
excerpt_fa: A study by Northeastern University and Consumer Reports found that automakers are collecting data to allow advertisers to build in-depth profiles on consumers.
content_en:
Study finds many new cars share your data with third-party companies
The report analyzed traffic from 21 vehicles and 30 automaker apps.
Pinterest probably doesn't need your car's VIN, but General Motors' apps were sending it there anyway — and to Snap, Yahoo, Meta, Google and the data broker Acxiom. At least, that's according to a recent study from Northeastern University, which tested 21 late-model cars and 30 automaker apps on Consumer Reports' fleet between October 2024 and August 2025.
Nineteen of those cars sent data to at least one third-party company via Wi-Fi, with seven of the apps passing identifiers like VINs, email addresses and precise locations to advertising and analytics companies. Four of those seven belong to GM, which has been under a 20-year FTC privacy order since January.
Those four GM apps are myCadillac, myChevrolet, myBuick and myGMC, and each sent VINs to 10 companies including Microsoft and Adobe. Meanwhile, HondaLink sent VINs and location to the analytics firm Amplitude, with the Lincoln and MyNISSAN apps making up the remainder of the list. But unlike a phone's advertising ID, a VIN can't be reset, so pairing one with an email address lets ad companies tie an owner to activity on other apps and websites.
According to Consumer Reports' per-vehicle summary, 10 of the 21 cars contacted no advertising or tracking domains on their own. The Buick Envista and Nissan Ariya were among them, yet pairing their apps exposed owners to 23 and 25 ad and tracking companies respectively. Tesla went the opposite way, with the Model 3 reaching 22 such companies from the car while its app added two. Since the team couldn't decrypt vehicle traffic and could only capture cellular data from the Model 3, these cars' real totals are likely to be higher. For most of the cars tested, the bulk of the ad-tech exposure came from the phone app. Meanwhile, 28 of the 30 apps contacted at least one advertising or analytics company, according to Consumer Reports.
Automakers point to vendor contracts and privacy policies
Back in January, the FTC finalized GM's punishment over its driver data sharing scandal. It handed down an order banning the company from selling driver data for five years to consumer reporting agencies, and says GM must receive express consent before it collects or shares connected vehicle data. It's important to note that Northeastern's testing predates that order, and the researchers haven't alleged a breach of it. GM told Northeastern Global News that it only discloses data to service providers that are contractually barred from selling or using it for their own purposes.
That aside, the researchers did approach 17 manufacturers with their findings and heard back from 14, all of which said the data flows matched their vendor contracts. Seven said it's ultimately the responsibility of the owner to read and accept the terms for every third-party service in the car, including pre-installed software, while five attributed the tracking to web pages opened inside their apps.
The researchers also read the privacy policies of the seven apps that shared identifiers, finding that each disclosed that it may pass personal data to third parties, without saying which ones or why. Owners who decline Tesla's data sharing agreement are warned of "reduced functionality, serious damage, or interoperability," while Rivian says that switching off data collection will limit or disable features like navigation and over-the-air updates.
Honda seems to be the only one willing to change anything, asking Amplitude to delete the location data and updating HondaLink to stop sending it, which a Honda spokesperson confirmed to Northeastern Global News. Northeastern professor and study co-author David Choffnes told the outlet that regulators should step in.

title_en: SpaceXAI's Grok: What's free in 2026 and what isn't?
title_fa: SpaceXAI's Grok: What's free in 2026 and what isn't?
excerpt_en: As with most AI tools, Grok's free tier is pretty limited.
excerpt_fa: As with most AI tools, Grok's free tier is pretty limited.
content_en:
SpaceXAI's Grok: What's free in 2026 and what isn't?
As with most AI tools, Grok's free tier is pretty limited.
Grok is one of 3,500 competing frontier AI models, most of which come with a variety of subscription plans, services and capabilities. But is Grok free, or does it follow the familiar approach of strictly limited free tiers and capabilities that other generative AI chatbots use? The short answer is yes, Grok is free, but the no-cost tier is basically a limited way to give the chatbot a try or make the occasional query.
You can use Grok without paying a dime through Grok's web and mobile experiences, and the free tier will cover things like basic chats, voice interactions and access to some web and X search features. Usage is capped, however, so frequent users will run up against that wall quickly. Free access offers a lightweight experience while paid subscriptions raise usage limitations and unlock more capable models and tools.
Of course, the exact quota is constantly subject to change, given current demand and xAI's plan rules, so never assume that "free" means unlimited back-and-forth or many of the same model choices premium subscribers have access to. Free users should also view Grok's widely-advertised and discussed image and video features as premium tools only. Some free knick-knacks are available here and there, but the most impactful generative media tools and the newest models are linked to paid plans.
What you get with Grok's paid plans
The most popular consumer upgrade is SuperGrok, and it's designed for those who want much higher usage caps, access to the more advanced models, longer conversations and priority access for any new features that drop. On xAI's plan page, SuperGrok is marketed as the "full power" version of Grok with access to improved models and higher rate limits.
Paid Grok AI subscription tiers include advanced reasoning models, image or video generation, coding tools and priority access during the busiest parts of the day. Business and Enterprise plans are a different category and are intended for organizations that require centralized billing and security controls or API-style deployment. Generally speaking, SuperGrok is for regular, individual users, while the SuperGrok Heavy tier is for people with unusually demanding workloads or who want access to the most resource-intensive models.
Business and Enterprise plans are a different category, and they're mostly intended for businesses that require centralized billing and API-style deployment. Neither is the optimal choice for an individual who just wants a solid chat model or heavy research tool. SuperGrok and enhanced Grok access also overlap with X subscriptions. SuperGrok Heavy includes X Premium, and X Premium users have access to some of Grok's more advanced features, including higher priority access.
Is SuperGrok worth paying for?
That depends on how you use AI. If you're just asking a question or two here and there or want to test out Grok's personality, the free tier will suit you just fine. If you find yourself heavily researching topics, writing code, generating more media than usual or you're constantly hitting limits, SuperGrok may be worth a shot.
Like most AI options, paid plans buy access and capacity. Unfortunately, your hard-earned dollars won't purchase 100 percent accuracy, which is an issue with all AI queries regardless of platform. Grok can still hallucinate or misread a prompt. It can produce claims that aren't entirely reliable, especially when the news is just dropping or a topic is trending on X. No matter what tier you choose to go with, it's always a good idea to fact-check Grok's or any AI's results.
Evaluate Grok like anything else, starting with the free tier so you can see whether it will earn a place in your day-to-day. If you need the extended reasoning or higher quality and volume image generation, step up to the next tier.

title_en: Is 3D printing safe to do in your bedroom or home office?
title_fa: Is 3D printing safe to do in your bedroom or home office?
excerpt_en: 3D printers are everywhere, but where one should be placed in your home is something worth looking into.
excerpt_fa: 3D printers are everywhere, but where one should be placed in your home is something worth looking into.
content_en:
Is 3D printing safe to do in your bedroom or home office?
Even PLA releases particles and gases. Here's what that means for your bedroom, desk and home-office setup.
A 3D printer can be placed on your bedside table. That does not mean that it is a good place to run one. Each print can take hours, and sitting next to the printer means breathing in air that may contain its emissions.
Even common PLA filament emits airborne particles and gases when heated. That means that overnight bedroom printing isn't a good idea, and a home office requires a bit more planning than a corner of the desk. When considering whether a 3D printer is worth buying, space is as important as what you want to print.
Even PLA isn't emission-free
A printer can alter the air in a room without smoke being visible. According to the EPA, filament printers emit ultrafine particles that can reach deep into the respiratory system, as well as volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Some of those gases can be harmful when inhaled.
PLA is usually recommended as a safer option, and it can produce fewer particles than ABS. ABS was found to emit more particles than conventional PLA in a 2026 test of 17 commercial filaments, with emissions differing between brands. The picture can also change due to nozzle temperature and additives. While switching to PLA helps, it's not a get-out-of-jail-free card to spend all day by a running machine.
Human airway cells have also been exposed to emissions from PLA and ABS printers, and changes associated with inflammation and cellular stress have been observed. The tests were conducted in a laboratory, however. They did not determine what long-term exposure at home does to people, nor did they establish a safe level of exposure for a bedroom.
There are other issues with resin printers (those that use liquid resin instead of filament). The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) warns that uncured resin may lead to skin reactions or asthma. Additional exposure risks may occur during washing and curing of prints, particularly with the use of solvents.
Where should you actually put a 3D printer?
A separate room or workshop with ventilation that exhausts outdoors is better than a bedroom. A garage can be used as well, provided it's properly ventilated and humidity and temperature fluctuations won't ruin your prints. Keeping the machine away from your desk reduces the time spent right beside it, but distance alone doesn't replace ventilation.
For a home-office setup, an enclosure with exhaust ducted outside can capture emissions closer to the source, while an open window alone may draw in fresh air without reliably removing the particles and gases emitted by the printer. NIOSH suggests that emissions should be captured close to the printer and that time spent near it should be minimized while it's operating.
Filters have limits. HEPA filters are designed to capture particles, and activated carbon can filter some VOCs if there is sufficient carbon. Neither can make a poorly ventilated room automatically safe, and proper enclosures, ducting and replacement filters all increase costs.
For occasional printing, a local printing service might make more sense if there's no suitable place for a printer. NIOSH also recommends keeping printers away from flammable materials and having fire detection in printing areas.

title_en: Will the HomeView be Apple’s first smart home success?
title_fa: Will the HomeView be Apple’s first smart home success?
excerpt_en: Over the past couple of years, we’ve seen multiple reports that Apple was working on a new smart home product, but now it seems the product has a name and a launch date.
excerpt_fa: Over the past couple of years, we’ve seen multiple reports that Apple was working on a new smart home product, but now it seems the product has a name and a launch date.
content_en:
Apple will announce a new smart home hub on Tuesday called the HomeView, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.
Over the past couple of years, we’ve seen multiple reports that Apple was working on a new smart home product, but now it seems the product has a name and a launch date. Gurman described the HomeView as a Siri-powered device with a display and an A18 chip, allowing customers to control their other smart home devices.
The HomeView will reportedly be available in two models — one designed for countertops and the other to be mounted on walls.
This would be Apple’s most serious bet on the smart home to date, after it failed to get much traction for its HomeKit software framework or its HomePod smart speaker.
Gurman reports that on Tuesday, Apple will also be unveiling updated versions of two other home devices, namely the Apple TV set-top box and the HomePod mini. Earlier this week, he said that Apple plans to announce a partnership with LG to create a smart lock, a thermostat, and a doorbell.

title_en: Aaron Sorkin’s ‘Social Reckoning’ is off to a weak start
title_fa: Aaron Sorkin’s ‘Social Reckoning’ is off to a weak start
excerpt_en: What does this mean for a fall full of movies starring villainous tech CEOs?
excerpt_fa: What does this mean for a fall full of movies starring villainous tech CEOs?
content_en:
“The Social Reckoning,” Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network,” is on-track to make only $5.5 million at the domestic box office this weekend, according to Sunday estimates.
That’s below the already underwhelming $7 million to $8 million the studio had projected, and it means Sorkin’s new movie is unlikely to become a “Social Network”-sized hit. The earlier film had a $22 million opening weekend and made a total of $97 million domestically (and that’s at 2010 ticket prices). It also won Sorkin an Oscar and became one of most influential on-screen depictions of Silicon Valley and startup culture.
Beyond the fate of a single film, the weekend box office could also offer hints about audience excitement, or lack thereof, as we kick off a fall full of movies starring villainous, real-world tech CEOs. There’s Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” (which also opened this weekend), Nathan Fielder’s apparently uncategorizable Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” (coming next weekend!), and the OpenAI boardroom drama “Artificial” (which has a new distributor after being dropped by Amazon).
Outside of theaters, Netflix also has a series called “The Altruists” coming in November, telling the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the collapse of FTX.
As for “The Social Reckoning,” while “The Social Network” was a notable success, the theatrical landscape has changed significantly in the last 16 years. And where the first film focused on the excitement and drama of Facebook’s early days, the sequel is darker and heavier — it’s all about whistleblower Frances Haugen’s decision to leak what became known as the Facebook files.
So maybe a movie about Senate hearings and algorithm changes was never going to be a big hit. Or maybe “The Social Reckoning”’s real audience is among older moviegoers who have only returned sporadically to theaters. And I wonder if critiquing Facebook feels a bit less urgent to audiences who are more likely to be losing sleep over AI.
Maybe just as importantly, the new movie’s reviews just aren’t very good. (For what it’s worth, I enjoyed “The Social Reckoning” but will fully admit that it’s overloaded Sorkin’s trademark speechifying. And I couldn’t help dreaming about a version directed — like the original — by David Fincher, with a score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross.)
“Musk,” meanwhile, made $69,000 during its opening weekend in four theaters. It will roll out more broadly in the coming weeks, but given its length and subject matter, the documentary will probably reach many more viewers once it starts streaming on HBO Max.

title_en: A college in Illinois tried to cancel its Flock contact and it refused
title_fa: A college in Illinois tried to cancel its Flock contact and it refused
excerpt_en: In April of 2025, Elgin Community College had six Flock safety cameras installed to "enhance the safety and security of students." But by September of that year, the school's administration grew concerned that Flock was sharing data with Customs and Border Patrol, that camera...
excerpt_fa: In April of 2025, Elgin Community College had six Flock safety cameras installed to "enhance the safety and security of students." But by September of that year, the school's administration grew concerned that Flock was sharing data with Customs and Border Patrol, that camera...
content_en:
In April of 2025, Elgin Community College had six Flock safety cameras installed to “enhance the safety and security of students.” But by September of that year, the school’s administration grew concerned that Flock was sharing data with Customs and Border Patrol, that camera feeds were not properly secured, and that both law enforcement and the company’s employees were abusing access to the data.
A college in Illinois tried to cancel its Flock contact and it refused
Flock refused to take its cameras down so Elgin Community College covered them. The company snuck back to undo it.
Flock refused to take its cameras down so Elgin Community College covered them. The company snuck back to undo it.
So in October of 2025, Elgin Community College requested Flock to remove its cameras. According to Elgin’s President Peggy Heinrich, Flock rejected the request, saying it had not violated its contract. According to the Chicago Sun-Times, school officials reached out again in December, offered to pay for the remaining five months of the contract, and still requested that the cameras be removed. They were met with silence.
That’s when things took a strange and somewhat sinister turn. According to the Sun-Times:
Heinrich said Elgin Community College staff began to cover the cameras using black trash bags and zip ties so that they would not be able to capture footage. But workers in an unmarked vehicle, which Heinrich assumed belonged to Flock, repeatedly removed the coverings.
“We were kind of in a back and forth for a bit where we’d cover, and then when they’d come to service, they’d remove,” Heinrich said. “Then we’d cover and then they’d remove.”
This continued until April of this year when the college’s contract expired, and Flock removed the cameras.

title_en: Anbernic's next dual-screen handheld has the perfect aspect ratio for 3DS games
title_fa: Anbernic's next dual-screen handheld has the perfect aspect ratio for 3DS games
excerpt_en: The RG DDS's main display has a 5:3 aspect ratio while its bottom screen will be 4:3.
excerpt_fa: The RG DDS's main display has a 5:3 aspect ratio while its bottom screen will be 4:3.
content_en:
Anbernic's next dual-screen handheld has the perfect aspect ratio for 3DS games
The RG DDS’s main display has a 5:3 aspect ratio while its bottom screen will be 4:3.
It's only been a year since Anbernic teased its remake of the Nintendo DS but the handheld company is already moving on to a contemporary version of its successor. Anbernic revealed the RG DDS, which is short for "Dream Dual-Screen" and an obvious nod to the Nintendo 3DS.
Improving on its predecessor, the RG DS, Anbernic went with Qualcomm's Snapdragon G2 Gen 2 chip. That means the RG DDS should handle emulating even up to Nintendo Switch and PlayStation 2 titles. Equipped with two displays, most gamers are likely going to replay 3DS favorites because of its matching aspect ratios. Anbernic built the clamshell handheld with a 4.7-inch main display that has a 1,200 x 720 resolution for a 5:3 aspect ratio and paired it with a 4-inch secondary display with a 960 x 720 resolution for a 4:3 aspect ratio. Anbernic hasn't revealed the rest of its upcoming handheld's internals, outside having a 6,000mAh battery.
As for the controls, the RG DDS is almost an exact match to Nintendo's handheld, but Anbernic added an extra analog stick on the right side. The dual-screen device even has an extendable capacitive stylus that can be tucked away when not in use. Anbernic also said there's a dedicated AI button, but hasn't yet detailed exactly what features it activates.
As usual, the handheld maker excluded any pricing or release dates in the reveal, but we're expecting the RG DDS to be a little more expensive than its $99 precursor. However, Anbernic is known for its affordability so it could potentially undercut the recently-released Retroid Pocket Duo and its Lite model that starts at $149.

title_en: The iPhone clock app has an oddity not many people know about
title_fa: The iPhone clock app has an oddity not many people know about
excerpt_en: Sure, you can set your iPhone's alarm to any time you choose. But there's a hidden limit to how far your choices will stretch, though most users won't reach it.
excerpt_fa: Sure, you can set your iPhone's alarm to any time you choose. But there's a hidden limit to how far your choices will stretch, though most users won't reach it.
content_en:
The iPhone clock app has an oddity not many people know about
There’s a limit to how far your alarm settings will scroll, and most people never reach it.
The iPhone Clock app has been around since the original iPhone launched 19 years ago, and for most, it's always been a fairly straightforward default app. However, there's a small curiosity hiding within the alarm settings that went viral in mid-2025, along with another quirk we'll talk about below. To put it simply, the alarm hour and minute scrolls seem infinite at first glance, but rapidly scrolling through the hours and minutes will eventually reach a dead end at 4:39. For those with a preference for military time, it ends at 16:39. Go ahead, give it a try and see for yourself.
Open the Clock app, select Alarms, tap the + button and start scrolling through the hours and minutes until you reach the end. It will take several swipes, but not too many if you scroll through as fast as you can, which is the reason why most people never noticed it in the first place. However, this little endpoint doesn't mean you're limited in setting alarms.
So why does the iPhone alarm stop at 4:39? The specific hour and minute seem a little strange and random, right? Well, Apple hasn't weighed in on this, but reports and online discussions offer differing explanations, like something called Tableview that an X user thinks is involved. For the most part, just treat it as an interesting idiosyncrasy. The numbers don't add up to 23 or anything, so there's no need to delve into conspiracy theories.
The icon tells time
Who knew? But seriously, there's another little detail here that's easier to spot once you know where to look. The Clock app icon isn't static. It tells you the current time, including a moving second hand. Apple introduced this feature in iOS 7, back when we were still grunting and finger painting on cave walls. If you've always opened the app to look at the time, you never really had to.
Also, there's an even subtler feature alluded to in the opening paragraph. Normally, the second hand moves in a continuous "sweeping" motion all the way around. On iOS 26.1 devices and later, however, Low Power Mode changes the motion to a once-per-second tick, like a traditional quartz clock. It still tells the time, of course, only with a less fluid animation. This is only a visual change, and there's no audible ticking involved.
If you're looking for one more option that's hidden in plain sight, open Stopwatch inside the iPhone Clock app and swipe across the display. You can switch between digital and analog stopwatch faces without installing another app. Unlike the alarm's endpoint, this is a documented feature that's included in the iPhone user guide.
How do I change the appearance of the clock app on my iPhone?
Now that the Clock's dirty laundry is out in the open, how about changing the app's appearance? Both the worst and the best iPhones offer a few clock-display options, though they're far from the aesthetic variety offered by other apps.
If you want a large bedside alarm clock, connect your iPhone to a charger and stand it up on its side. This places it in StandBy mode, which displays widgets, photos or just a good old-fashioned clock. Change the types of clocks displayed by swiping to the left or right.
Last but not least, you can enable Night Mode so StandBy mode adapts to the low-light environment of a typical bedroom when it's sleepy time. The screen will display a heavy red tint, so it's a little less intrusive, especially if the bedside table is level with your face. It's not a mysterious oddity or anything, but there it is.
However, if you expect your iPhone to behave exactly like a standard bedside clock, you'll need to make sure Always-On Display is active in Settings. It works best to slap a MagSafe charger with a kickstand on the back. Some older iPhones don't have Always-On Display, so you'll have to give the screen a little nudge to turn it on or you can pester Siri about it.

title_en: Silicon Valley is falling in line with Trump’s attempt to rename AI
title_fa: Silicon Valley is falling in line with Trump’s attempt to rename AI
excerpt_en: When President Donald Trump announced his plans to rebrand artificial intelligence as "super intelligence," you'd be forgiven for being skeptical that it would catch on. While most of the broader population is sticking with AI, some of Silicon Valley's most powerful are falling...
excerpt_fa: When President Donald Trump announced his plans to rebrand artificial intelligence as "super intelligence," you'd be forgiven for being skeptical that it would catch on. While most of the broader population is sticking with AI, some of Silicon Valley's most powerful are falling...
content_en:
When President Donald Trump announced his plans to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence,” you’d be forgiven for being skeptical that it would catch on. While most of the broader population is sticking with AI, some of Silicon Valley’s most powerful are falling in line and trying to give Trump the great AI rebrand he so desires.
Silicon Valley is falling in line with Trump’s attempt to rename AI
Musk, Benioff, Huang, and now Nadella have all capitulated to Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ rebrand.
Musk, Benioff, Huang, and now Nadella have all capitulated to Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ rebrand.
That Elon Musk was quick to jump on board, promising to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, isn’t surprising. When, hours after Donald Trump declared that “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” Marc Benioff announced that Salesforce would rename AIForce to SIForce; it seemed like a quick capitulation, but not entirely out of character.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang attended the summit where the executive order requiring government agencies to use the term “super intelligence” was announced. He’s also aligned himself with Trump, saying he believes the danger posed by AI is overblown. So it was somewhat predictable that when Nvidia declared that it would “commit” $1 billion to scientific advancement, that included “super intelligence research.” Of course, Huang has a lot to lose if he gets on Trump’s bad side.
The latest to cave is Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, who attended the same AI summit as Huang along with Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Jeff Bezos, Dario Amodei, and Musk. In a post calling for building an “emergency brake” for AI yesterday, Nadella repeatedly referred to the technology as “super intelligence.”
During Trump’s second term, Silicon Valley has repeatedly tried to ingratiate itself with the administration, after having a much more contentious relationship during his first term.

title_en: Steam Frame teardown reveals one problem with its future repairs
title_fa: Steam Frame teardown reveals one problem with its future repairs
excerpt_en: In an otherwise repairable device, the cooling fan is hard to reach.
excerpt_fa: In an otherwise repairable device, the cooling fan is hard to reach.
content_en:
Steam Frame teardown reveals one problem with its future repairs
In an otherwise repairable device, the cooling fan is hard to reach.
Although the Steam Frame is too expensive and late to the party to bring the masses into VR, it does a lot of things right. That includes its repairability. But iFixit's teardown flagged one component that isn't easy enough to reach: the cooling fan.
The problem? That fan is buried deep inside the headset. To get to it, you have to snake past the optical assemblies, making your way through a dense jungle of thermal hardware, cables and other components. While the fan and heat pipe are separate (a good thing), getting there in the first place is more of a problem.
That's a lot of disassembly for a part that may need cleaning over time. After all, fans accumulate dust, and they eventually wear out. Burying one this deep makes the Steam Frame a harder repair than it otherwise might have been.
A blemish on an otherwise smooth repair path
Fortunately, repairs elsewhere are a much more encouraging story. The Steam Frame's head strap detaches via quick-release latches, making it easier to work on the rear battery pack without messing with the displays. In a win for hygiene, the sweat-absorbing parts are replaceable, including the nose bridge and face and headrest cushions.
The lenses attach magnetically to the headset's IPD rail, making display and eye tracking repairs relatively straightforward. (Removing them does still require some disassembly, including screws and cables.) Overall, it's a fairly approachable repair by VR standards. No digging out the motherboard required.
There are a few other catches. The headset's battery lacks release tabs. (iFixit removed it using isopropyl alcohol and some gentle prying.) In addition, the controllers' thumbsticks are soldered to their boards, so replacing a broken one would be more involved than you might hope.
You'll eventually be able to buy replacement parts from iFixit's store. (Although iFixit is also Valve's repair partner, it says the headset maker had no input on the teardown or editorial process.) However, the company says replacement batteries won't be available when its Steam Frame parts store goes live. That seems like a pretty big omission, and it's one that iFixit says it hopes to change. Replacement displays also won't be available at launch. Of course, Valve does offer warranty repairs and replacements for covered devices, but that doesn't negate the importance of DIY support.
Can't fix that price
Overall, iFixit's teardown reveals a surprisingly repairable VR headset. But whether you want to buy one is another matter. Starting at $1,059, the Steam Frame costs considerably more than the Meta Quest 3. And it does so without delivering an equivalently upgraded experience.
To be fair, it is a powerful and comfortable headset with many perks. It has standalone support for many Steam games, including the excellent Half-Life: Alyx. It also offers wireless PC streaming and microSD expansion. But on the whole, it feels like a headset that would have made more sense several years ago, when developers were investing more resources in VR software. The Steam Frame's high price (thanks, RAMageddon!) combined with that late arrival makes it a tough sell, despite the solid repairability.
You can read more about the Steam Frame in Devindra Hardawar's review.

title_en: The meaning behind the padlock symbol in your PlayStation 5 game library
title_fa: The meaning behind the padlock symbol in your PlayStation 5 game library
excerpt_en: Digital game licenses aren't perfect, which is why you might see a padlock icon blocking you from PS5 games.
excerpt_fa: Digital game licenses aren't perfect, which is why you might see a padlock icon blocking you from PS5 games.
content_en:
The meaning behind the padlock symbol in your PlayStation 5 game library
Being locked out of your own games isn't fun, but there are solutions to get back in.
Sony's plans to stop making disc-based games beginning in January 2028 mean digital games need to work flawlessly. Unfortunately, that's not always the case. On your PS5, you may have found some titles inaccessible, as evidenced by a padlock icon over their thumbnails. From your perspective, this can be baffling. You've paid for a game and installed it, so it should always be ready to play, right?
The reality is that when you buy a game from an online store, you typically don't get permanent ownership rights — just a license to download and play. Sony has final control over how you access games associated with your account. If the company withdraws a license for whatever reason, or something goes wrong with the authentication process, you're blocked from accessing the title. This is what the padlock indicates.
As if that weren't enough, the way PlayStation Store and Plus subscriptions work can create headaches. Thankfully, there are some methods to fix those padlocks.
Fixing the PlayStation padlock icon
First, check that you're signed into the right PlayStation account, since that's what ties all your purchases and subscriptions together. You can sign out of an account by going to Settings > Users and Accounts > Other > Sign Out, or sign back in via Settings > Users and Accounts > Account > Sign in. This menu lets you create new accounts if needed, too. Next, confirm that PlayStation Network is online using the PlayStation Status page. If PSN is down, you may get locked out of games.
You'll also want to verify that PSN recognizes your purchases, or in the case of PlayStation Plus, that you both have an active subscription and the game you want to play is included with it. Titles are added and removed on a regular basis, so you'll see a padlock on games you previously downloaded that aren't in the library anymore (as well as if your subscription has lapsed).
Scan your transaction history at Settings > Users and Accounts > Account > Payment and Subscriptions > Transaction History. As for Plus, your status is under Settings > Users and Accounts > Account > Payment and Subscriptions > Subscriptions, and you can browse the PlayStation Plus website for the current library.
When multiple people share a console, it's possible to play another person's games under your own account. This is known as "gamesharing," and works as long the owner has Console Sharing and Offline Play enabled under Settings > Users and Accounts > Other. That option can only be enabled on one PS5 at a time per account, so if the owner has multiple consoles, they may need to re-designate the one you're on.
If you know you should have direct or shared access to a game, you may need to force PSN to restore licenses. Go to the game in your library, press the Options button on your controller, then select Restore License. You can also go to Settings > Users and Accounts > Other > Restore Licenses to fix multiple games simultaneously.
What if your PS5 games are still locked up?
Before moving forward, restart your PS5 (press the PS Button on your controller, then go to the Power menu and choose Restart PS5). You should also install any available updates at Settings > System > System Software > System Software Update and Settings. Bugs fixed by the latest patches don't typically affect licensing issues, but it's good to rule everything out.
Finally, if you see the padlock icon on a disc-based game, that means the disc isn't acting as a "key" to authenticate the title. Confirm sure the correct disc is inserted into your console. Eject it and make sure it's clean and inserted the right way (label facing up if the console is horizontal, or to the left if it's vertical).
Beyond these, in an extreme scenario, there could be a glitch with your PS5's database. You can attempt to solve this by booting your console into Safe Mode. Follow these steps:
- Turn off the system by holding the Power button on its front until you hear a second beep, which takes a few seconds.
- Once the console shuts down, press and keep holding the Power button again. Release it only after you hear two beeps, the second of which should trigger in seven seconds.
- Connect your controller via a USB cable, then press the PS Button on the controller.
- Once Safe Mode is running, select Clear Cache and Rebuild Database.
Should that not accomplish anything, it's time to talk to PlayStation Support.

content_en:
The latest rumors are that the new Apple TV will have a built-in microphone, while the upgraded remote will get a speaker. The mic would let users control the set-top box using Siri without having to speak into the remote or a connected HomePod device. That could also let the Apple TV serve as a simple smart home hub — controlling thermostats and locking doors — without the need to hunt for the remote.
The new Apple TV could have a built-in mic and a remote with a speaker
The overdue Apple TV refresh makes it easier to talk to Siri and find your remote.
The overdue Apple TV refresh makes it easier to talk to Siri and find your remote.
If you happen to misplace the remote, the new integrated speaker should make it easier to track down. It could play an audio alert to guide you to its location, whether it got carelessly kicked under the couch or a child mischievously hid it in a drawer.
This is on top of the upgrade to an A19 chip that will power Siri AI. The Apple TV is expected to start shipping on October 30th, alongside the refreshed HomePod Mini.

title_en: Can the AI industry persuade data center opponents by getting rid of NDAs?
title_fa: Can the AI industry persuade data center opponents by getting rid of NDAs?
excerpt_en: On Equity, we debate the impact of data center moratoriums and whether the AI industry has a communication problem.
excerpt_fa: On Equity, we debate the impact of data center moratoriums and whether the AI industry has a communication problem.
content_en:
Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Sean O’Kane, Rebeccan Bellan and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities.
Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried.
Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication.
“We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said.
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
Sean O’Kane: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular.
There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. etc.
I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point.
This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip.
The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too.
So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now.
Rebecca Bellan: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco, which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years.
But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this.
Anthony Ha: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York. I believe it’s a one year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.]
So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.”
But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried.
It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs. I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it. I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step.
Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right? This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc.
And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant. But we’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them. And that’s because, a lot of time, the [technological] ability’s not there, and in part...

title_en: Why strong magnets can hinder the iPhone's rear-facing camera
title_fa: Why strong magnets can hinder the iPhone's rear-facing camera
excerpt_en: Magnetic accessories can be handy, but make sure they're not interfering with your camera.
excerpt_fa: Magnetic accessories can be handy, but make sure they're not interfering with your camera.
content_en:
Why strong magnets can hinder the iPhone's rear-facing camera
Magnetic accessories can be handy, but make sure they're not interfering with your camera.
Apple continues to up its camera game. This September, Apple debuted its iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, a lineup which introduced its most advanced camera system to date. The new 48-megapixel Fusion Main camera comes with variable aperture, low-light sensor and pro controls that render sharper shots for amateurs and professionals alike. But what if I told you that your phone's accessories could ruin these photos outright?
Frequently, your favorite iPhone accessory depends on strong magnets and magnetized metal plates to stick to your phone's casing. Whether you're using a removable grip, car mount, power bank or ring lights, you are potentially placing strong magnetic fields. And while they likely don't affect your phone's internal systems, Apple has found that these magnets interfere with your phone's camera.
This occurs because the rear-facing cameras on your iPhone use image stabilization technologies to prevent blurring and preserve focus. Such lens-position sensors are hypersensitive to magnetic fields and may become disabled when near certain accessories. On its support page, Apple suggests magnetic accessories may cause your camera's images to blur. Other auxiliary factors, such as exposure to high amplitude vibrations, such as those produced by high-powered motorcycles, can also cause lasting damage to these camera sensors.
All about the magnets
Your iPhone relies on two magnet-sensitive lens-positioning sensor technologies to stabilize your camera's pictures. The first is known as optical image stabilization, or OIS, which uses a gyroscope to sense the movements of your camera when taking a photo. If you move while taking a photo, your OIS will reduce how much the image blurs by adjusting the lens to match the gyroscope's movements. In doing so, OIS reduces image motion, allowing you to take sharp, crisp images.
The second, known as closed-loop autofocus, prevents gravity and vibrations from causing motion blur through onboard accelerometers, a form of magnetic sensor that measures these outside factors and compensates your camera's lens position. By adjusting its lenses' focus, your iPhone can preserve the sharpness in your videos, panoramas, and camera stills.

title_en: Apple's smart home hub will reportedly be called HomeView
title_fa: Apple's smart home hub will reportedly be called HomeView
excerpt_en: Bloomberg reported that the HomeView device will start shipping in November.
excerpt_fa: Bloomberg reported that the HomeView device will start shipping in November.
content_en:
Apple's smart home hub will reportedly be called HomeView
Bloomberg reported that the HomeView device will start shipping in November.
Just ahead of Apple's smart home event on Tuesday, we may finally have a name for the long-awaited smart home hub. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the device that will serve as a Siri command center for a user's Apple-powered smart home will be called the "HomeView" and will make its big debut during the company's "Welcome home" event.
The smart home hub is expected to pair with Apple's other smart home devices, like the HomePod mini that's also expected to get a refresh. However, Gurman explained that the "View" portion of the name is meant to convey that the device will be a display that is primarily controlled through Siri and voice commands, instead of something like "HomePad," which would imply a tablet experience.
According to Gurman, the HomeView will come in a countertop version with a metal speaker base in space gray, silver, starlight and pink color options, as well as a wall-mounted model that will only come in space gray and silver. Unlike Apple's other hardware, the HomeView will only support a limited selection of Apple apps and won't have access to the App Store, Gurman reported. Instead, Apple reportedly wants users to lean on third-party accessories that can connect to the HomeView device through Siri, Apple's Home app or its devices.
To achieve that, Apple has been working with LG to develop several smart home devices, including doorbells, thermostats, outdoor security cameras and more. Gurman also reported that Apple is working with Schneider Electric SE for smart home devices across the European market, but that all of these third-party products will be available under the "Apple Home Collection."
To go along with the reported HomeView hub, Apple is expected to reveal a revamped HomePod mini with the S10 chip and a new Apple TV set-top box with the A19 chip, Gurman said. While the new HomePod mini and Apple TV are expected to start shipping and be available in Apple stores on October 30, the HomeView will release a few weeks later in mid-November, according to Gurman. The third-party products from LG should release after that, with Gurman predicting they will ship later this year at the earliest.
