title_en: Petra Power looks to modernize energy for data centers and defense vehicles
title_fa: Petra Power looks to modernize energy for data centers and defense vehicles
excerpt_en: The startup says its fuel cells are super efficient and cut fuel costs during a time when the tech industry can’t get enough electricity.
excerpt_fa: The startup says its fuel cells are super efficient and cut fuel costs during a time when the tech industry can’t get enough electricity.
content_en:
As AI gobbles up an ever larger amount of energy, the hunt is on for efficient and cost-effective power sources. One of the companies leading the charge is Petra Power.
Petra, which was founded in 2017, sells solid oxide fuel cells — ceramic devices that convert fuel, like natural gas, into electric power without burning it. The company markets them as a more efficient and environmentally friendly way to operate data centers and large vehicles.
Petra’s founder, Aaron Goodman, told TechCrunch that his company’s product has significantly lower fuel costs and emissions than traditional power sources, and that they have much less of a physical footprint, too, because they’re more compact and lightweight.
The efficiency, and the cost savings that come with it, is what makes the fuel cells attractive. “Combustion takes fuel and creates explosions,” Goodman said, describing how traditional power generation works. “Those explosions create heat. That heat creates motion. The motion powers an electromotive force, which eventually creates electricity. It’s a lot of steps, and they all have so much loss in them that you end up with a really inefficient system.”
Petra’s fuel cells skip most of these steps. “What fuel cells do is they take the electrons directly off of the fuel, so they strip the fuel of its electrons, which creates electricity,” he explained. “It’s one step, no loss, and subsequently, in theory, at least, they’re much, much more efficient.”
As a result, companies that run off fuel cells stand to save a significant amount on fuel costs, Goodman said.
Although it may offer an innovative product, the customer base is still emerging for Petra. Goodman said that his company is targeting two different types of customers: data centers and the Defense Department.
Goodman doesn’t want to reveal specific agreements just yet, but said Petra is currently working with neoclouds and other infrastructure providers that were a few steps down from the hyperscaler crowd. The target for first deployment with these customers is 2028, with full-scale production for the company hopefully set for 2029, Goodman said.
“Hyperscalers are an ICP [ideal customer profile] for us, and we talk a lot to them, but we don’t have anything firm with them yet,” said Goodman. “We’re still kind of working in that direction. Obviously, they’re the largest consumers of power. They’re the ones that we can make the biggest impact with, so that’s where we’d like to go.”
The other customer — the government — is also still taking shape. The idea is that Petra’s fuel cells will be able to provide auxiliary power for land vehicles, meaning electricity for onboard equipment when the main engine is off. But Petra’s product has not actually deployed on a live vehicle yet, Goodman clarified. Instead, the fuel cells are in the testing phase, during which the government is deciding whether to move forward, he said.
Petra is a small team — some 15 people — but the company is growing, Goodman said. Petra has so far received nearly $9 million in contracts from the Defense Department, and the hope is to scale that work significantly in the coming years, he said.
Petra Power was selected for this year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200, a group of 200 startups chosen for the program. You can catch all the action this coming week in downtown San Francisco at Moscone West.

title_en: Ledger wallet tampering suspected after reports of crypto thefts
title_fa: Ledger wallet tampering suspected after reports of crypto thefts
excerpt_en: Reports have been mounting that users of the Ledger crypto wallet have seen their accounts drained, and it appears to be related to tampered hardware sold by CryptoBillis. Ledger has asked CryptoBillis to pause all sales of its wallets while it conducts an investigation. Ledger...
excerpt_fa: Reports have been mounting that users of the Ledger crypto wallet have seen their accounts drained, and it appears to be related to tampered hardware sold by CryptoBillis. Ledger has asked CryptoBillis to pause all sales of its wallets while it conducts an investigation. Ledger...
content_en:
Reports have been mounting that users of the Ledger crypto wallet have seen their accounts drained, and it appears to be related to tampered hardware sold by CryptoBillis. Ledger has asked CryptoBillis to pause all sales of its wallets while it conducts an investigation. Ledger has confirmed that “one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant.”
Ledger wallet tampering suspected after reports of crypto thefts
A spy implant in some Ledger crypto wallets may be the root of an $86 million supply chain attack.
A spy implant in some Ledger crypto wallets may be the root of an $86 million supply chain attack.
Photos and videos posted on X and Threads appear to show a small circuit board sandwiched under the screen. The implant allegedly intercepts anything displayed on the screen, including the seed passphrase shown during the initial setup. Using an embedded SIM card, the implant then sends that information back to the attacker, who can then siphon funds from user accounts.
Reports indicate that whoever is behind the hack has stolen over $86 million worth of crypto from hundreds of wallets. There’s no indication that Ledger’s systems have been compromised or that wallets purchased directly from the company have been affected. Instead, the issue appears to be a supply chain attack primarily involving users in Southeast Asia and the CryptoBillis reseller. Ledger has provided guidance on how to check if your wallet has been tampered with.
Update October 10th, 2026: Added additional statment from Ledger.

title_en: How to reset your Samsung TV
title_fa: How to reset your Samsung TV
excerpt_en: If you have a Frame TV or one of the other Samsung models, you may occasionally need to reboot or factory reset it.
excerpt_fa: If you have a Frame TV or one of the other Samsung models, you may occasionally need to reboot or factory reset it.
content_en:
How to reset your Samsung TV
If your Frame or other Samsung TV is acting up, give these resets a try,
Resetting devices is, oddly enough, an essential skill in the modern tech landscape. Aside from the fact that selling or trading devices like smartphones and laptops is incredibly common, it's an effective troubleshooting technique. Factory resets force a device to revert to its out-of-the-box state, including options, processes and installed apps. It can be a royal pain to get things back the way you like — but it's better than dealing with crashes or broken features.
There are few reasons to reset a smart TV, including Samsung models, yet things do sometimes go haywire. A favorite streaming app might repeatedly freeze no matter how many times you reinstall it, or the OS might develop problems like video glitches. There's no guarantee that a reset will come to the rescue, but it's a good troubleshooting step.
There's not much to performing one on a Samsung TV. Just be sure to try simpler tactics first, some of which we'll go over later. Remember, once you've triggered a factory reset, there's no going back. On top of reconfiguring picture and sound preferences, you'll be redownloading apps and OS updates.
All you need to know about factory resetting your Samsung TV
Before initiating a factory reset, be sure you have any PIN codes and passwords written down somewhere, including the logins for streaming apps and your Wi-Fi router. Once the reset is complete, you'll need these to get back to watching anything. Unless, perhaps, you're content with over-the-air TV, Blu-ray or a connected game console or PC. Even then, you may want to get back online briefly to install updates for Tizen, Samsung's OS.
Once you're sure you want to go ahead, follow these steps:
1. From the home screen, select Settings.
2. Click All Settings.
3. Choose General & Privacy.
4. At the very bottom of the menu, click Reset.
5. You'll need to enter a PIN, even if you haven't created one. If you haven't chosen a custom PIN, enter 0000.
6. Select OK. Your TV should begin the reset process a moment later.
Periodically, Samsung updates Tizen in a way that relabels certain buttons and menus. As a rule, though, the process shouldn't vary much from generation to generation. Just look for similar-sounding labels, and explore a bit if you have to.
If you're apprehensive about going nuclear, there are some soft resets you can try first. For minor or one-off glitches, these may be all you need. Some are specific to particular problems, though, as you'll see.
The soft reset options for Samsung TVs
To simply reboot your TV, unplug it for 30 seconds or hold the power button on the remote for five seconds. Your TV will briefly turn off, then pop back on with the Samsung logo. A reboot might not seem very dramatic, but this does clear out your TV's RAM and system cache. It also restarts background processes, which can sometimes glitch out.
You might, in rare cases, benefit from resetting the Smart Hub without performing a full factory reset. This reverts the Hub's options to defaults and wipes associated apps and account info. You'll have to redownload apps and log in again. To reset the Hub, follow these steps:
1. Go to Settings > All Settings.
2. Click Support.
3. Choose Device Care, then Self Diagnosis.
4. Click Reset Smart Hub.
5. Enter your PIN. If you didn't choose one, enter 0000.
Lastly, you might try resetting network settings if you're specifically dealing with connection issues. Chances are the problem lies with your router or service provider, so troubleshoot those first. It can't hurt to reconnect with a fresh start, however, as long as you have your router's login info handy. Here's the process:
1. Head to Settings > All Settings.
2. Click Connections, then Network.
3. Choose Reset Network. To confirm, click Reset.
4. Return to Network Settings to enter your router's SSID and password.
You might understand now why you'd want to jump straight to a factory reset if a reboot doesn't work. If an issue is hard to diagnose, a total reset can save you the hassle of resetting components one by one. There's also nothing to be lost unless you simply can't remember a critical login.

title_en: Cloudflare acquires Deno to improve its Workers programming model
title_fa: Cloudflare acquires Deno to improve its Workers programming model
excerpt_en: Cloudflare will use this acquisition to improve its Workers programming model and platform.
excerpt_fa: Cloudflare will use this acquisition to improve its Workers programming model and platform.
content_en:
Cloudflare announced Friday that it’s acquiring Deno, the startup behind the programming runtime of the same name.
According to Cloudflare’s Kenton Varda, Cloudflare will use this acquisition to improve its Workers programming model and platform, which allows customers to build and run software on Cloudflare’s network. (Varda is principal engineer for Cloudflare Workers.)
Deno — which was co-founded by Bert Belder and Node.js creator Ryan Dahl — recently launched celld, an open source implementation of Workers, which Varda wrote “delighted” the Cloudflare team. Varda argued that contrary to “a popular theory” that the company “made Cloudflare Workers work differently from other cloud platforms in order to create ‘lock-in,’” the company believes “being open source and giving people an escape hatch is good business.”
Dahl, meanwhile, wrote that his team is “joining Cloudflare to make the Workers programming model a mainstream way to build servers.”
The financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. Deno had raised a total of $26 million, including a Series A led by Sequoia.

The financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. Deno had raised a total of $26 million, including a Series A led by Sequoia.

title_en: GameStop is hoping PS5 Pro buyers are desperate enough to pay $500 over MSRP
title_fa: GameStop is hoping PS5 Pro buyers are desperate enough to pay $500 over MSRP
excerpt_en: A shortage has driven resale prices through the roof.
excerpt_fa: A shortage has driven resale prices through the roof.
content_en:
GameStop is hoping PS5 Pro buyers are desperate enough to pay $500 over MSRP
A used PS5 Pro will run you about $1,400.
As the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 approaches, gamers are scrambling to maximize gameplay with the most advanced consoles on the market. Advertised as PS5 Pro Enhanced, the game comes as Sony faces a shortage of its popular console. With the AI boom consuming the world's silicon, Sony has struggled to maintain its production cycles, leading to a global shortage of the console that is likely to last well into 2027.
Released in 2024, Sony now prices its advanced console $200 higher than its initial asking price, listing it at a whopping $899.99. However, you may end up paying well above this already inflated price tag if you are looking to snag a new console by the end of the year. As it stands, retailers and resellers alike are taking the laws of supply and demand to heart. GameStop, for instance, currently lists a used PlayStation 5 Pro for an eye-popping $1,399.99, half a grand over its MSRP. Similar markups can be found across the resale market.
Sony has attempted to dampen these markups where it can. In Japan, for instance, the company instituted a lottery system tied to game time minimums, presumably to rein in a reseller market that is quickly getting out of control. However, with no end to the shortage in sight, inflated prices are only likely to persist.
A runaway market
The PS5 Pro is indicative of broader trends in the consumer tech market. Data centers are gobbling up high-bandwidth memory, a key component for delivering data quickly to advanced processors. The cascading effect has seen the production of the dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) necessary for consumer devices like the PS5 Pro lag, sparking shortages. An August 2026 JP Morgan report predicted that by the end of the year, the price of DRAM will have risen 400 percent worldwide since the PS5 Pro was released in 2024.
These trends are likely to persist. In September 2026, German gaming publication Playfront reported that internal memos between Sony and its distribution partners state that the PS5 Pro shortage would persist "through early 2027 at the earliest." Some expect the component constraints to persist far beyond next year, with some forecasting that the RAM crisis could persist until the 2030.
GameStop is just one of several sellers attempting to squeeze every last drop out of the PlayStation 5 Pro shortage. Best Buy, for instance, is currently selling the console for over $1,500. Walmart, meanwhile, is selling an open box version of the console for $1,200. These prices are largely in line with the resale market, with prices on eBay regularly soaring above $1,100. For what its worth, GameStop owns roughly 10 percent of the online marketplace, and attempted a $56 billion unsolicited takeover of the company earlier this year.
The exorbitant prices sparked by Sony's PlayStation 5 Pro crisis are quickly becoming the norm for most consumer tech products. According to a September 2026 report by The Economist, the consumer price index for "computer software and accessories" skyrocketed by 31 percent. In addition to the PS5 Pro's $200 increase, PlayStation 5s have increased by $150, roughly 30 percent. Such trends could prove catastrophic for the industry. This month, video game hardware sales hit a 13-year low.
Is it worth the pricetag?
Before splurging on GameStop's PS5 Pro, you may want to ask whether the upgrade is worth the cash. Capable of running 4K graphics at 60 frames per second, the PS5 Pro's enhanced visuals look great on a high-end television. Add 2 TB of memory, an enhanced GPU and special features like ray tracing, andthe PS5 Pro delivers tangible advantages over its predecessor.
The greatest advancement is its PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) image upscaler, which uses AI to enhance image pixels. Although somewhat maligned at its initial release, PlayStation made an improved edition, PSSR Enhanced, that is now the console's default setting. However, like many of the Pro's most compelling features, PSSR only works for games labeled PS5 Pro Enhanced, like GTA VI. To date, however, you and a friend could probably count the number of games that natively use the new PSSR on your hands. Whether these visual upgrades meaningfully change the gaming experience, though, is debated.
Sony's latest PS5 update may begin to narrow the gap between the two consoles. In an October 2026 blog post, Sony stated that it was bringing a similar AI upscaling functionality known as Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) to the PS5. Although not described by Sony as the "gold standard" of PSSR, QSSR will bring image and stability improvements to the PS5.
Overall, the PlayStation 5 Pro is a more powerful, visually compelling console to its predecessor. However, many reviewers already questioned whether these enhancements were worth the PS5 Pro's initial price tag. Given that GameStop is selling the advanced console for nearly double the 2024 asking price, and $500 above MSRP, its safe to say that breaking the bank for the PS5 Pro likely isn't worth it.

title_en: How Xiaomi, Oppo and other non-US brands are challenging the iPhone Duo
title_fa: How Xiaomi, Oppo and other non-US brands are challenging the iPhone Duo
excerpt_en: Apple's foldable phone has everyone talking, but competitors have their own offerings in different ways.
excerpt_fa: Apple's foldable phone has everyone talking, but competitors have their own offerings in different ways.
content_en:
How Xiaomi, Oppo and other non-US brands are challenging the iPhone Duo
The foldable phone market heats up as new competitors emerge.
While Apple is already selling the iPhone 18 Pro, the world is waiting for the iPhone Duo — the first foldable iPhone. It won't hit stores until October 23, with pre-orders beginning a week earlier.
But Apple's competitors have had their eyes on it for quite some time. In fact, the market has been gearing up for the iPhone Duo long before Apple even officially announced it. That's no wonder, since there was a lot of anticipation about what exactly Apple would do differently in the foldable device world that's been around for some time now.
The competition will be fierce: Xiaomi, Oppo, Motorola and Samsung are just a few examples of companies that have been exploring the idea of foldable phones that look a lot like the iPhone Duo. And like the Duo, most of them now have a foldable device in a "passport" format. But will that be enough to compete with Apple?
Xiaomi and Samsung went wide first
The Xiaomi 18 Fold arrived just days before the iPhone Duo was unveiled, and specs-wise, they're quite similar. Both have a 7.6-inch inner screen and a 5.4-inch outer screen with the same aspect ratio, giving the phone a passport-like shape. But there are a few areas where the Xiaomi 18 Fold comes out on top: it's lighter than the iPhone Duo, weighing 219 grams compared to the iPhone's 254 grams.
The Chinese brand is also betting on a better camera setup, with three lenses on the back. iPhone users who opt for the Duo will miss out on that extra optical zoom range. The price is also more aggressive: Xiaomi's foldable phone starts at 10,999 yuan (about $1,640), but it will only be available in China for now.
In the US, the iPhone Duo's main competitor is likely to be Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold8. The new base Z Fold ditches the near-square design of previous models in favor of the wider "passport" shape, with 7.6-inch and 5.5-inch screens. Unlike Xiaomi, Samsung opted for a straighter design with no curved corners. Our review gave it an 8.9 out of 10 and called it a better device for watching shows and movies than the more expensive Z Fold8 Ultra, which keeps the original square-ish shape. It also has two rear cameras, like Apple's model.
The Z Fold8 definitely turned heads after its launch in August, but the Duo could put an end to that. Samsung's offering begins at $1,900, only $100 less than the iPhone Duo's starting price.
Oppo and Motorola push battery and charging
Oppo's Find N6 took a different approach. It kept the more conventional foldable design seen in devices like the Z Fold8 Ultra, with a 6.62-inch outer display and an 8.12-inch inner display. But its standout feature is its thinness; it's just 8.93mm thick when closed, much closer to the 8.75mm of an iPhone 18 Pro. The Duo measures 11.3 mm when closed.
And if battery life is a major concern, you'll appreciate the Oppo being packed with a 6,000mAh battery — that's 1,600mAh more than the Z Fold7. It also supports 80W wired fast charging. If that's not enough, the Find N6 includes IP59 certification and a 200-megapixel main camera. While targeted at the Asian market, there is a "global model" that should work in other parts of the world, though it's not officially for sale in the US. It also costs less than the iPhone Duo, starting at 9,999 yuan (about $1,490).
The Motorola Razr Fold is another option you can find in US stores, and one that utilizes a more conventional foldable design. It has a 6.6-inch outer screen that unfolds into an 8.1-inch inner screen with an impressive peak brightness of 6,000 nits (compared to the iPhone Duo's max of 3,000 nits). It also comes with a massive 6,000mAh battery, 80W charging and a triple-camera system, so you get optical zoom for photos and videos. The inner display also supports a stylus (a $100 add-on), with the Razr Fold starting at $1,900.
So while the competition is tough, Apple has shown it's ready to compete with the iPhone Duo. Many of its best tricks come down to software. iOS 27 comes with plenty of optimizations for the foldable form factor, including cool animations when you switch between displays and varied usage modes.

content_en:
TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 starts in just three days. Moscone West is getting ready, hundreds of startups are preparing to show what they’ve built, and thousands of founders, investors, and tech leaders are heading to San Francisco.
The three-day countdown is on, and so are your pass savings of up to $100. Grab your pass before TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 doors open on October 13 at 8 a.m. PT. Bring a co-founder, colleague, or peer and get a second ticket of the same type at 50% off. Coming with a group? Enjoy even more savings when you register four or more attendees.
Discover the next breakout company at Disrupt
For more than a decade, discovering ambitious early-stage companies has been at the heart of Disrupt. Startup Battlefield 200 puts a handpicked group of early-stage startups in front of investors, media, potential customers, and the wider technology ecosystem, with 20 finalists taking to the Disrupt Stage to compete for the $100,000 prize and the coveted Disrupt Cup.
300+ showcasing startups
You don’t need to follow the competition to make startup discovery the focus of your visit. Throughout the Expo Hall, over 300 startups at different stages and from different sectors will be showing what they’re building, giving you the chance to talk directly with founders and find a startup, product, investment opportunity, or idea you weren’t expecting.
200+ sessions and 250+ tech leaders shaping the conversations
Or, if you want to combine discovery with content, explore 200+ sessions led by 250+ tech leaders across six stages, plus roundtables and breakouts. Covering AI, product, GTM, fundraising, finance, infrastructure, and scaling, these sessions give you the chance to ask questions, spark new connections, and hear industry announcements and insights before they hit the mainstream.

You can still access the opportunities at Disrupt with an Expo+ Pass for just $75. Attending with colleagues or friends? Bring a group of four or more and unlock additional savings.

content_en:
Sunmi is an undeniable force in K-pop. She first made her debut as a member of the Wonder Girls back in 2007, one of the first K-pop acts to really break through in the West. The English version of their single “Nobody” was the first K-pop song to hit the Billboard Hot 100 in October 2009.
K-pop star Sunmi loves Notion and ear cleaning videos
Nearly 20 years into her music career Wonder Girls’ Sunmi is staying humble, but persistent.
K-pop star Sunmi loves Notion and ear cleaning videos
Nearly 20 years into her music career Wonder Girls’ Sunmi is staying humble, but persistent.
In 2010 Sunmi left the group to go back to school, but the siren call of a music career pulled her back in. She released her debut solo EP Full Moon in 2014. That began a run of award-winning releases for the pop star, including Song of the Year for “Gashina” at the Gaon Chart Music Awards.
Despite her near-constant presence in the K-pop world as a solo artist and as a member of the Wonder Girls, whom she rejoined in 2015, Sumni only just released her first solo LP, Heart Maid, in 2025. This year she released the single “Forever July,” which blends ’90s R&B synths with rubbery bass and UK garage-inspired drums. Sunmi has called it one of her most personal songs. And she wasn’t afraid to get personal in our Q&A either, revealing details about her writing process, her greatest disappointment as an artist, and her love of ear cleaning videos.
What is your most indispensable tool?
My phone. I use the Notes app and Voice Memos a lot when I’m writing lyrics or making music. Whenever I have a good idea, I can immediately pull it out and write it down, so I really can’t live without it.
Which is the most underappreciated?
The Samsung Galaxy series. It has made my work environment so much easier.
Team Galaxyyyyyy!
What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?
These days, you can transfer all the apps and data from your previous device, so I don’t really have to install anything separately. But if that process didn’t exist, I’d probably install KakaoTalk, a messaging app, first.
What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?
I have so many unnecessary photos and screenshots in my gallery. I wish there were a feature that could recognize similar or duplicate photos and group them together, so I could delete them all at once.
What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?
Notion. I use it a lot because I work on many group projects. It’s convenient, but it takes quite a long time to get used to. I think the UI could use some improvement.
How many tabs do you have open right now?
Four: Notion, Google Drive, YouTube, and Claude.
Which social media platform do you use the most?
I don’t really use social media that much, but I think I use Instagram and X the most.
What is your happy place online?
Videos of people getting their ears cleaned on YouTube.
What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?
I’m not really good with technology, but I think the Samsung Z Fold 8 that I’m using right now is probably my favorite device. I often need to work on documents or edit videos while I’m on the go, and it’s incredibly convenient. I can work with both hands on a wide screen, and it’s surprisingly light. It’s exactly the kind of device I’ve always needed.
What game do you have the fondest memories of?
MapleStory by Nexon. I played it when I was in elementary school, and even after becoming an adult, I would sometimes play the mobile version. The graphics really bring back memories of my childhood.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
Deepfakes. Ew.
What is one thing you wish you had created?
Stranger Things 5 and Game of Thrones 8.
What creation are you most proud of?
“Tail.” It’s a song that still gets me excited every time I perform it live. When I hold my breath, the audience holds their breath too, and when I explode, they explode with me. It creates this really unique experience.
Which are you least proud of?
“You Can’t Sit with Us.” It was the first song where I ever tried rapping. But the lyrics and even my voice were terrible.
What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?
Always stay humble. You should never let yourself become arrogant.
What is your current obsession?
I really love ice cream. Korean summers are shockingly hot, so it’s hard to survive without ice cream. I absolutely love Salt & Straw’s Salted Caramel Waffle Cone, but there’s nothing quite like it in Korea.
What do you do when you need to focus?
I find a small space to organize my thoughts.
What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?
I say “No?” out loud. For example, if I start thinking to myself, “I can’t do this,” I immediately say “No?” out loud.
When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?
When I’m shooting, I leave my phone with my manager. Even during short breaks, I barely look at my phone. But I’ve never actually gone somewhere without my phone.
What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?
The Senses of an Everydayist, a new essay collection by lyricist Kim Eana. She sent me a copy as a gift when it was published, but I believe there’s something meaningful about personally buying and reading someone’s creative work, so I bought a copy online.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
A meal with the people I love.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
Dancing on the Borderline.
What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

My phone. I use the Notes app and Voice Memos a lot when I’m writing lyrics or making music. Whenever I have a good idea, I can immediately pull it out and write it down, so I really can’t live without it.
Which is the most underappreciated?
The Samsung Galaxy series. It has made my work environment so much easier.
Team Galaxyyyyyy!
What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?
These days, you can transfer all the apps and data from your previous device, so I don’t really have to install anything separately. But if that process didn’t exist, I’d probably install KakaoTalk, a messaging app, first.
What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?
I have so many unnecessary photos and screenshots in my gallery. I wish there were a feature that could recognize similar or duplicate photos and group them together, so I could delete them all at once.
What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?
Notion. I use it a lot because I work on many group projects. It’s convenient, but it takes quite a long time to get used to. I think the UI could use some improvement.
How many tabs do you have open right now?
Four: Notion, Google Drive, YouTube, and Claude.
Which social media platform do you use the most?
I don’t really use social media that much, but I think I use Instagram and X the most.
What is your happy place online?
Videos of people getting their ears cleaned on YouTube.
What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?
I’m not really good with technology, but I think the Samsung Z Fold 8 that I’m using right now is probably my favorite device. I often need to work on documents or edit videos while I’m on the go, and it’s incredibly convenient. I can work with both hands on a wide screen, and it’s surprisingly light. It’s exactly the kind of device I’ve always needed.
What game do you have the fondest memories of?
MapleStory by Nexon. I played it when I was in elementary school, and even after becoming an adult, I would sometimes play the mobile version. The graphics really bring back memories of my childhood.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
Deepfakes. Ew.
What is one thing you wish you had created?
Stranger Things 5 and Game of Thrones 8.
What creation are you most proud of?
“Tail.” It’s a song that still gets me excited every time I perform it live. When I hold my breath, the audience holds their breath too, and when I explode, they explode with me. It creates this really unique experience.
Which are you least proud of?
“You Can’t Sit with Us.” It was the first song where I ever tried rapping. But the lyrics and even my voice were terrible.
What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?
Always stay humble. You should never let yourself become arrogant.
What is your current obsession?
I really love ice cream. Korean summers are shockingly hot, so it’s hard to survive without ice cream. I absolutely love Salt & Straw’s Salted Caramel Waffle Cone, but there’s nothing quite like it in Korea.
What do you do when you need to focus?
I find a small space to organize my thoughts.
What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?
I say “No?” out loud. For example, if I start thinking to myself, “I can’t do this,” I immediately say “No?” out loud.
When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?
When I’m shooting, I leave my phone with my manager. Even during short breaks, I barely look at my phone. But I’ve never actually gone somewhere without my phone.
What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?
The Senses of an Everydayist, a new essay collection by lyricist Kim Eana. She sent me a copy as a gift when it was published, but I believe there’s something meaningful about personally buying and reading someone’s creative work, so I bought a copy online.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
A meal with the people I love.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
Dancing on the Borderline.
What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

title_en: 5 Samsung Galaxy features you should be using after updating to One UI 9
title_fa: 5 Samsung Galaxy features you should be using after updating to One UI 9
excerpt_en: Samsung Galaxy phones that have upgraded to Android 17 and One UI 9 have a slew of new features - some more helpful than others.
excerpt_fa: Samsung Galaxy phones that have upgraded to Android 17 and One UI 9 have a slew of new features - some more helpful than others.
content_en:
5 Samsung Galaxy features you should be using after updating to One UI 9
One of them is a pretty useful security feature.
With its latest crop of foldables in August came Samsung's One UI 9 update, the first version of the company's interface for Galaxy devices to be built atop Android 17. Along with a fresh new version of the operating system, One UI 9 brings some welcome updates and features. It's rolling out widely as of this writing to recent flagships prepped for the update.
By now, we've grown accustomed to a slew of sloppy AI features accompanying new smartphones, so it's a great relief to report that many of the new inclusions this time around seem like things real people might actually appreciate. Even some AI features are a bit more grounded than the gimmicky photo generation features from the past couple of years.
After installing One UI 9 on both a Galaxy S26 Ultra and S25 Ultra, we tested its most exciting new features to figure out which are the most useful. While some features seemed great on paper, like the Now Nudge feature that's supposed to serve up contextual information when you need it, they turned out to be lackluster in practice. Now Nudge still hasn't shown me anything useful, even with a scary amount of my data being fed into it. On the other hand, some of the more pedestrian additions to the software turned out to be quite handy. Here are the five Samsung Galaxy features you should be using after updating to One UI 9.
My FanCam lets you turn a wide video into a tracking shot
Samsung has spent a lot of effort on AI photo and video editing features you've probably never touched, but now it seems to be homing in on the things people will find useful. One of the marquee features in One UI 9 is My FanCam, which lets you turn a wide shot into a tight tracking shot of a single person. One marketing clip from Samsung shows a video of a rock band, and when My FanCam is invoked, each of the band's members is highlighted on screen. Once the user chooses the guitarist, the video crops around him in close-up.
Aside from concerts, the feature is perfect when shooting dance videos for social media. Rather than being forced to stay in the frame of a vertically shot video, you can dance in widescreen and then crop to the vertical framing afterward. It also seems like a promising way to get highlights of your kids' sports games. My FanCam will simply track a subject across an entire video, and you don't need to shoot video in a specialized mode to make it work. The magic happens when you open a video you've already recorded in Samsung Gallery and tap the Galaxy AI button, which is an icon that looks like sparkles.
AI-powered video editing apps like CapCut have offered similar functionality for years, so the fact that you can now produce the same thing natively in Samsung's Android software is a welcome addition. Accomplishing this kind of tracking shot in a manual editing program like Adobe Premiere Pro can require hours of tedious work, so it's remarkable to see this automatic capability run on a smartphone. Blessedly, the feature works on-device without sending data to the cloud. In Engadget's testing, My FanCam was available and worked while the phone was in airplane mode. You will, however, need a Samsung account login. Engadget tested the feature on a Galaxy S26 Ultra and S25 Ultra, but One UI 9 is still in the process of rolling out to older models. Outside reporting shows that Galaxy phones in the S24 series are the oldest models to have My FanCam in the beta version of One UI 9.
Even more Quick Panel customization
Customizing your phone is easier in One UI 9. With One UI 7 in 2024, Samsung visually overhauled One UI, and among the biggest changes was the decision to split quick settings and notifications into two different panels. One UI 8 and 8.5 went even further by allowing users to customize the Quick Panel, as it's called. Settings can be placed anywhere they fit, and they can even be resized. Now, in One UI 9, Samsung is giving users even more control.
The biggest change this time around is to the volume and brightness sliders. Yes, you could reorient them vertically before, but the volume slider always had the ringer mute shortcut glued to one end. The same was true of the brightness slider and dark mode toggle. Now, you can ditch those buttons and turn the sliders into solo operators. Sliders in general are now also more minimal, shimmying free of the large UI pads around their borders in previous software versions. Borders around tiles have also been nixed.
The most subtle change is to the music player widget that lives in the Quick Panel (though it also appears atop the notifications panel and in the live notification chip in the top left of the screen). The little waveform that appears on the scrubber bar during playback now matches the current album art.
Better document scanning helps flatten the curve
For many years, Samsung has offered a document-scanning feature inside its native One UI camera app. It's one of the most convenient ways to quickly scan paper documents, signage and more. But it does struggle with curved surfaces, making it difficult to scan book pages or anything else that doesn't lie completely flat.
In One UI 9, Samsung gave the document scanner a major upgrade that should help it to digitize books and other bound documents more accurately, as well as documents with folded corners. Previously, if a document appeared warped after scanning it with the camera, there were a few tweaks you could make after the fact to help smooth it out, but the odds of doing so successfully weren't great. Ditto for folded paper, in which case dog-ears and other folds showed up as harsh lines in the scanned photo. In One UI 9, the scanner will automatically compensate for both scenarios, meaning you can scan two pages of a book and it will look like a flat, digital render of the pages rather than like a reading packet handed out by your high school English...

title_en: Anthropic is cutting off its internal evaluations from the internet
title_fa: Anthropic is cutting off its internal evaluations from the internet
excerpt_en: After a recent spate of high-profile incidents in which AI agents escaped containment, Anthropic is cutting off internet access for all internal evaluations. In a report Friday, the company detailed "unintended model actions," including submitting a false tip regarding an...
excerpt_fa: After a recent spate of high-profile incidents in which AI agents escaped containment, Anthropic is cutting off internet access for all internal evaluations. In a report Friday, the company detailed "unintended model actions," including submitting a false tip regarding an...
content_en:
After a recent spate of high-profile incidents in which AI agents escaped containment, Anthropic is cutting off internet access for all internal evaluations. In a report Friday, the company detailed “unintended model actions,” including submitting a false tip regarding an unsolved murder, that led to the decision.
Anthropic is cutting off its internal evaluations from the internet
Anthropic is is keeping its agents offline during testing until it can prevent ‘unintended model actions.’
Anthropic is is keeping its agents offline during testing until it can prevent ‘unintended model actions.’
Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures (described in the remediation section of this post) reliably catch behaviors like these.
The ability to gain access to the live internet, even when models were supposed to be operating in isolation, has been an ongoing issue for AI companies. Many incidents, including the Hugging Face attack, involved agents that were supposed to be denied access to the internet. Yet, in case after case, the agents found creative solutions to bypass those restrictions. Physically removing internet access would certainly improve security around AI testing, but it would also limit its usefulness.
The report also amounts to an admission that Anthropic is often unaware of what its agents are doing and does not have a reliable system for monitoring their behavior. Cutting off internet access is just the latest action the company has taken to try and rein in its agents, including temporarily pausing training its frontier models.

title_en: Why your smart speaker keeps misunderstanding you (and how to fix it)
title_fa: Why your smart speaker keeps misunderstanding you (and how to fix it)
excerpt_en: Smart speakers should recognize your voice to run commands, but you can help them out with a few tricks.
excerpt_fa: Smart speakers should recognize your voice to run commands, but you can help them out with a few tricks.
content_en:
Why your smart speaker keeps misunderstanding you (and how to fix it)
Smart speakers have gotten better at comprehending you, but they don't get it right every time.
Because smart speakers are so convenient, you notice little annoyances right away when they stop working so smoothly. A common issue is your speaker misunderstanding you, whether due to your proximity to the speaker or other noise in the house. Luckily, these issues are pretty simple to fix.
Many of the fixes are common across top smart speaker models, while each of the big names (Google Home, Apple HomePod and Amazon Echo/Alexa) require some specific know-how to reduce misunderstanding.
Universal methods to improve understanding with smart speakers
First, check that your speaker is clean. Use a dry cloth to wipe the unit down if there's a buildup of dust or gunk. If issues persist, try moving your speaker to another spot or an entirely different room. Background noise, echoes and distance (whether too close or too far from your own voice) can all make a big difference. Try to avoid having smart speakers near regular noise sources like fans or surround sound speakers. Ideally, keep it at least one foot away from walls.
Having multiple speaker units can also cause issues if one taking your request isn't the closest. If the app allows, try lowering the sensitivity of the problematic speaker. For Echo devices, you can change the wake word per-device to avoid activating the wrong one. Failing those fixes, try to keep devices as physically separated as you can.
After shifting it around, test a few voice commands to see if there's a marked difference in its comprehension. It's also worth checking that you're issuing a command your speaker is actually able to execute. And of course, be sure you're speaking clearly and concisely.
When working with other smart products, make sure your linked smart home devices have unique names. Your speakers can mistake one device for another if multiple have a similar title. Use a few unique words in each name for maximum clarity, and give each room a clear label in your home app as well.
Specific fixes for Alexa, Google Home and HomePod
If your speaker is still failing to understand your commands properly, it might be time to play with some settings. The best change is setting up voice recognition so the assistant has an easier time recognizing the way you speak. For an Echo, open the Alexa app and navigate to More > Settings > Account Management > Your Profile > Voice ID, where the app will ask you to say various commands to set up a Voice ID it recognizes across platforms.
For Google-powered speakers, open the Google Home app and head to Settings > Google Assistant > Voice Match to set up Voice Match for all of your connected devices. You can have up to six distinct voices per home.
For an Apple HomePod speaker, open the Home app and tap the More button (three dots) to access Home Settings. There, open your user profile and turn on Recognize My Voice. For a smoother experience across devices, open Settings on your phone, tap your name at the top of the page, then go to iCloud. Tap See All by Saved to iCloud, then enable Siri.
If none of these methods improve your issue, restart your speaker by unplugging it for a minute and then plugging it back in. If you suspect a major issue, you may need to go a step further and perform a factory reset. This will reset all your custom settings, so only do this if nothing else has worked.

excerpt_en: Today, I’m talking with Peter Kafka, chief correspondent at Business Insider and host of the Channels podcast, about the gigantic Warner Bros.-Paramount merger and the future of the company now simply called Skydance. Skydance is owned by David Ellison, son of Oracle CEO Larry...
excerpt_fa: Today, I’m talking with Peter Kafka, chief correspondent at Business Insider and host of the Channels podcast, about the gigantic Warner Bros.-Paramount merger and the future of the company now simply called Skydance. Skydance is owned by David Ellison, son of Oracle CEO Larry...
content_en:
Today, I’m talking with Peter Kafka, chief correspondent at Business Insider and host of the Channels podcast, about the gigantic Warner Bros.-Paramount merger and the future of the company now simply called Skydance.
Will Warner Bros. kill Skydance — or will David Ellison kill Warner Bros?
Maybe the thi— no, fou— wait, fifth time’s the charm for WB.
Skydance is owned by David Ellison, son of Oracle CEO Larry Ellison, and its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery officially closed the day Peter and I spoke.
There are some grand ambitions here, but the reality is that acquiring Warner never goes well for anyone. AOL failed, AT&T failed, and Discovery failed — although it did succeed in flipping these assets to Skydance. So I wanted to ask Peter if he thinks the Ellisons and Skydance have a real shot at succeeding where so many companies before them have hit the rocks.
Okay: Peter Kafka on Warner Bros. and Skydance. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Peter Kafka, you’re the chief correspondent at Business Insider, and you’re the host of the Channels podcast, our sister podcast here on the Vox Media Podcast Network. Welcome back to Decoder.
Thanks for having me. It’s big media day again!
A big media day. It’s an auspicious day, as my parents would say. It is the day that the Warner-Paramount merger closes. We’ve all been calling it Warner Mount, but I’m told this company will instead just be called Skydance.
Skydance!
Every time I see the word Skydance, I assume it is foreign-owned, which is maybe true in some way.
Another way to think of it is that there are iconic names in Hollywood. Paramount is such an iconic name that Viacom turned itself into Paramount years ago. Warner Bros. is a legendary studio. Let’s get rid of those names. Let’s add Skydance, which no one’s ever heard of.
Let’s just start at the start. There was Paramount. There’s Warner Bros. The deal closes today. That is all going to be a new company called Skydance. Is Skydance just a holding company? Are we as consumers meant to know that this thing exists?
I think for the near term, you’re still gonna think of companies like Paramount, Warner Bros., and HBO as brands you know, but this is going to be one company. They’re going to merge everything. They’re likely going to merge the streaming services, Paramount and HBO, into a thing, not right away, but eventually. So I do think Skydance will be a name that consumers will probably know at some point.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
I just have to ask, what are the chances that HBO Max will be rebranded yet again into Skydance?
There’s probably gonna be some branding stuff. Not again. In the near term, because this is still a cable TV company, there are actually some limits on what these guys can do with their brands and their services. And they won’t come out and say, “We’re gonna mush this stuff together.”
But there’s likely to be one mega streaming service, and maybe you can get HBO separately, or maybe you can only get HBO or only Paramount. Still, it’s gonna be one thing, and one movie studio. It’s all gonna get mushed together, and it’s all gonna be run by David Ellison.
David Ellison is just the latest to believe that he can buy Warner Bros. and make something good happen. I have joked many times on this show that maybe the only antitrust policy this country needs is to make it illegal to buy Warner Bros., and that would just solve a lot of problems. Why does he think he will be successful?
Well, his dad’s the eighth richest man in the world, so that’s not nothing.
That Oracle stock is tied up in a bunch of AI stuff. It’s moving up and down.
We can talk about that. But one, that means that he literally has the money to buy this, and two, that this is a public company kind of in name only. David Ellison and Larry Ellison, his father, control this company effectively. They don’t really need to worry that much about equity shareholders. Debt’s a different issue.
And he’s 43. He’s got a long run backed by tens of billions of dollars of his father’s money to take a stab at this. And as you said, he will not be the first person to do this. There’s a long list of failures. I think maybe that’s appealing to guys like him. It’s like, “Everyone else is dumb. I’m the smart guy who’s gonna figure it out.”
“Everyone else is dumb, and I’m smarter than everyone else is,” is very appealing. But that long list of failures, if you just look at it — they’re all shaped like this idea. We’re gonna take iconic Warner Bros. content, we’re gonna marry it to new distribution, we’re gonna reduce the overhead and costs and decadence of Hollywood. Where does new revenue come from?
There’s no plan for new revenue. There’s no announced plan for new revenue. Right now it’s shrinking; it’s cutting costs. title_en: How to change your home address on Google Maps
title_fa: How to change your home address on Google Maps
excerpt_en: Set it to a nearby place instead, if you're concerned about the potential dangers if someone accesses your phone.
excerpt_fa: Set it to a nearby place instead, if you're concerned about the potential dangers if someone accesses your phone.
content_en:
How to change your home address on Google Maps
Think of the time you'll save.
No matter where you navigate with Google Maps, you always return home eventually. Because it's the destination you travel to most, it makes sense to have quick access to your home address to cut down on wasted time. Thankfully, Google Maps has special shortcuts for your home, as well as other frequently visited locations.
If you've recently moved or have never set your home address, take a moment to configure it now. You can do so on the web or mobile app. Before you do this, though, consider the security implications of having your home address stored in your phone. If your device was stolen, or even if someone was able to snoop around for a minute, they could easily check your exact address by opening Google Maps (or other apps where you save this information, like Uber).
To enjoy the conveniences this feature provides without potentially exposing your full address, consider saving your "home" as a nearby public place like a restaurant or grocery store. That way, navigation is close enough that you'll know how to get home from there.
Set your home address using Google Maps on the web
Open Google Maps in a browser, then click Sign in at the top-right if you're not already logged in. When you click inside the search box, you should see Home and Work entries at the top, where you can select Edit to change them.
If not, click your profile icon at the top-right and choose Manage your Google Account. On the resulting page, click Personal info on the left sidebar, then scroll down to find and choose Home address. If you don't already have an address set, enter yours here and Maps will offer autocomplete suggestions.
The Address line 2 button is available if needed, or you can hit Choose on map if pinpointing your desired destination is preferable to typing it. This is also helpful for finding a nearby public place to save instead of your home address. In case you don't want to keep this information anymore, choose Remove. While you're here, you might want to also enter or update your Work address. That keeps it easily accessible in Google Maps and provides commute estimates.
Change your home address using the Google Maps app
In the Google Maps app on Android or iPhone, tap the You icon on the bottom bar. On the page that appears, choose the list called Labeled on the page that appears. If you don't see it, tap the More arrow to see all your lists. In the Labeled list, you should see Home and Work entries.
To change either address, tap the three-dot button next to it and select Edit home (or Edit work). Enter your new address using the bar at the top, which should populate as you type. Use Choose on map if, again, you prefer dragging a pin around or if your home location doesn't map cleanly to an address.
For a bit of fun, try the Change icon action for either of these special addresses. You can tweak them to stand out with options like a treehouse, submarine, or barn. And if you don't want to use this feature anymore, tap Remove to clear the address.
Labels and contact addresses are great, too
With labels, you assign a custom name to any spot, which you can then search for or use in voice commands for a better Android Auto experience. These are great for frequently visited places. For example, you might use Gym as a friendly name instead of having to say "Navigate to Planet Fitness on Cherry Street" every time. It's also possible to label places without an address, like GPS coordinates for a specific campsite in a park. Try them for places that are easily confused with others or otherwise clumsy to type.
To label a place from your computer or laptop, click on the location to open its panel on Google Maps, scroll down and click Add a label. On your phone or tablet, scroll left on the row of small icons below the place's basic information, then chose More > Add label. Labeled places appear with their name and a blue icon on the map. Plus, the Labeled group is cleaner than lists since it doesn't include photos, review scores, opening hours and other such info. It just displays the name and icon you've chosen for each item and the address on file.
Finally, don't forget that Google Maps will show addresses you have saved for any of your contacts, letting you search for them by name. If this doesn't work, make sure you have your Google contacts synced with your phone and that the Google Maps app has access to your contacts.

title_en: How to take care of your foldable phone's hinge
title_fa: How to take care of your foldable phone's hinge
excerpt_en: Foldable phones require a little more care than standard ones, but the hinge will do its job as long as you don't make that difficult.
excerpt_fa: Foldable phones require a little more care than standard ones, but the hinge will do its job as long as you don't make that difficult.
content_en:
How to take care of your foldable phone's hinge
You don't need to baby a modern foldable, but a few boring habits can keep its hinge from becoming an expensive problem.
I've found that the durability of a foldable can be extremely unpredictable. I used my Galaxy Z Fold4 for almost three years, and it went through a lot of rough handling. My mom's Z Fold6 broke after about a year, with the inner display failing. Debris around the hinge may have been a factor, but the cause was never determined.
That's why I wouldn't take a manufacturer's fold-count rating as a "use-by" date. Modern hinges are engineered to last for years of normal use, while Google says the Pixel 10 Pro Fold's gearless hinge can handle over 10 years of folding. The idea isn't to ration every unfold, but to avoid making an already complex piece of hardware work harder than necessary.
Keep dirt out and let the hinge do its job
Maintaining a foldable hinge comes down to some fairly mundane practices. Keep grit away from it, make sure nothing is sitting between the displays before closing the phone and don't force the mechanism in a direction it clearly doesn't want to go.
Samsung advises that you clear away any foreign objects before closing its foldables, and to not apply too much pressure to the inner display. That's especially worth keeping in mind with phones like the Galaxy Z Fold8 and Z Flip8, which have IP48 ratings. The "4" indicates protection against solid foreign objects 1mm or larger, but it does not make the phones dustproof. A beach trip isn't a good time to discover how much grit your hinge can take.
Motorola is even more upfront about it, stating that dust can shorten hinge life and may cause damage to the internal display. It also suggests checking for debris before closing the phone and advises against using pressurized air dusters on the display.
But that doesn't mean you have to start counting every time you open the phone. Book-style foldables like the Pixel 10 Pro Fold can handle plenty of everyday tasks while folded. Flip phones naturally encourage more opening and closing, but newer models reduce that need. For instance, the Razr+ 2026 can run full apps on its 4-inch external display without being opened.
Fold-count claims aren't expiration dates
The giant numbers attached to foldable durability claims are reassuring, but remember that these are laboratory results, not a countdown to failure.
The OLED panel used in the Galaxy Z Fold7 remained fully functional after 500,000 folds during a 13-day Bureau Veritas test at 77 degrees Fahrenheit, Samsung Display said. That's equivalent to over 10 years of use if folded around 100 times per day, or over six years if folded more than 200 times per day.
There's an important distinction within that number, however: the test only covered the foldable OLED panel. Samsung Display didn't claim that every hinge component, flex cable or other part of the phone would last 500,000 cycles.
Real phones have a harder life than test equipment. They are dropped, left in dusty pockets, exposed to temperature fluctuations and sometimes come into contact with water. A foldable can have issues long before its folding mileage is reached, even if the hinge itself is not the part that fails.
Focusing on changes in the phone's feel is more helpful. Motorola says some noise from the hinge is normal, but if the mechanism becomes harder to move, stops opening normally or starts making new grinding noises, it's worth paying attention rather than forcing another fold. Ignoring that caution can cost you a lot: Samsung currently lists a Galaxy Z Fold8 inner-screen module replacement at $579.

title_en: Can you use a screen protector with your foldable phone?
title_fa: Can you use a screen protector with your foldable phone?
excerpt_en: Screen protectors seem like an easy win for keeping your phone in good condition, but there's more to consider with a foldable phone.
excerpt_fa: Screen protectors seem like an easy win for keeping your phone in good condition, but there's more to consider with a foldable phone.
content_en:
Can you use a screen protector with your foldable phone?
What you should know before applying a screen protector to your foldable phone.
Screen protectors are among the first accessories many people think about when buying a new phone. It's no wonder; they're a low-cost investment to protect an expensive purchase, and nobody wants permanent scratches on their phone's glass. Screen protectors for standard phones are standardized by now, but for foldables, it's more complicated.
Not only do most foldables have two screens, but the inner screen uses technologies different from those of standard displays. Foldables are more delicate, so understandably, people want to take extra care with them.
But what about screen protectors? Can you put one on a foldable phone? The short answer is yes, but it depends on the screen. It's fine to put a protector on the outer screen, but you should avoid putting anything on the inner display.
Why is the inner screen of foldable phones so fragile?
Due to the physics involved, the inner screen of a foldable smartphone doesn't use regular, rigid glass. Instead, it relies on many flexible layers to survive hundreds of thousands of folds — and to better protect all those layers, foldable phones usually come with a built-in screen protector.
On Samsung foldable phones like the Galaxy Z Fold8, the screen protector is made of TPU, which is flexible and specifically designed for foldable screens. The recently announced iPhone Duo, Apple's first foldable phone, also comes with a screen protector on top of the display layers. This protector also adds a nano-texture coating that gives the screen a matte finish and reduces the visibility of the crease.
Phone makers don't want you messing with the inner screen. When Samsung introduced the first Galaxy Fold, some people thought they could remove the screen protector on their own. As a result, the display began malfunctioning right after that, leading Samsung to warn consumers that the screen protector should not be removed. Samsung and Apple both offer replacements for this internal screen protector — but they have the right tools to do it. You shouldn't try to do this on your own. If the inner screen of your foldable phone looks worn, take it to an authorized repair center.
Some brands sell ultra-thin screen protectors for the inner screen of foldable phones, which are usually less than 0.1mm thick. Whether it's worth the risk is another matter, since companies make it clear that applying an unofficial screen protector to the inner screen can damage the entire display. For such expensive devices, the best approach is to follow the company's advice.
How to protect your foldable phone
The outer screen of a foldable phone is a different story. You can put any screen protector on it, since it's essentially a regular smartphone screen covered by a hard piece of glass. Modern smartphones are usually equipped with chemically strengthened glass, such as Gorilla Glass or Apple's Ceramic Shield, which provide extra protection against scratches and cracks. Still, if you want to add a screen protector for extra peace of mind, that's totally fine.
But as it turns out, scratches aren't the biggest enemy of a foldable phone; dust is. The latest Galaxy Z Fold devices, for example, are IP48-certified. That makes them resistant to short periods of water immersion and particles larger than 1mm, but they aren't completely sealed. The hinge mechanism is still fragile and vulnerable, and can end up getting damaged by small particles of dust or sand. Apple's iPhone Duo is IP68-certified, which means it's dust-tight and also resistant to dunks in water.
Still, only time will tell if it holds up as well as a regular smartphone, since this resistance is not permanent. Also, even if dust can't enter the device, small particles can still scratch the screen if they get inside and rub around. To protect your foldable phone, getting a case that covers the hinge is a better idea than using a screen protector on the inner screen. Avoid the most common foldable phone mistakes, and follow general advice to make your phone last longer, too.

excerpt_en: When it comes to TVs, the LG name has long been synonymous with OLEDs, continually leading Samsung and Sony as the top OLED manufacturer. But 2026 is all about RGB LED TVs. Almost every major company has released models with the new technology - including LG and its $3,600...

content_en:
When it comes to TVs, the LG name has long been synonymous with OLEDs, continually leading Samsung and Sony as the top OLED manufacturer. But 2026 is all about RGB LED TVs. Almost every major company has released models with the new technology — including LG and its $3,600 75-inch Micro RGB evo MRGB95B that I’ve been testing. And while LG’s RGB LED TV benefits from the brightness and color capability the technology provides, it has issues I couldn’t overlook that its less expensive competitors don’t.
LG’s RGB LED TV is good for certain situations, but an OLED is better
A bunch of little issues add up to make the MRGB95B not worth the price when competitors do it better.
A bunch of little issues add up to make the MRGB95B not worth the price when competitors do it better.
The MRGB95B comes in three sizes, with the 75-inch being the smallest. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports, supports Dolby Vision — although not Dolby Vision 2 or HDR10+ — and comes with the Magic Remote design LG unveiled last year. It has a more traditional remote shape instead of the curved wand of previous versions. As with all LG TVs, the MRGB95B runs on webOS. It runs quickly, but I find it less intuitive to navigate than Google TV, Apple TV, or Roku. It supports all of the major streaming apps.
The Good
- Bright picture
- Vibrant color
The Bad
- Some color inaccuracy out of the box
- Very distracting reflective screen
- More blooming than competitors
Speaking of software, a quick note: LG has recently come under increased scrutiny after a video from Gamers Nexus showed security vulnerabilities and continuous audio recording on its TVs, which LG has denied. When setting up the MRGB95B, it’s only necessary to accept the terms of use and privacy policy if you want to use webOS. Otherwise, as with any TV, it can be disconnected from the internet, although an external streaming device would be needed for any streaming services (I use an Apple TV 4K, myself).
OK, moving on. So, why buy an RGB LED TV?
RGB LED TVs use zones of individual red, green, and blue LEDs as backlights as opposed to a field of white or blue LEDs that rely on a color filter or quantum dots to create the colors that reach our eyes. RGB LED TVs have a color filter, too, but since the backlight is already creating color based on what’s needed onscreen, the color filter doesn’t need to work as hard to dial that in. It allows for higher color brightness and the ability to display more colors.
LG (and Samsung) use the term Micro RGB to describe the technology, while others say Mini RGB LED. And while the LG and Samsung RGBs are reportedly smaller (although neither has confirmed the exact size), it doesn’t directly translate into more zones or better performance over Mini RGB.
As with all of the RGB LED TVs I’ve seen this year, the 95B gets very bright — I measured a peak of 4,011 nits in HDR Filmmaker mode — allowing it to deliver an impactful image even in a sunlit living room. And in a dark room, the highlights in scenes from The Meg really pop. At the other end of the spectrum, though, the LG struggles a bit. Near-black shadow detail, such as the corners of the living room and kitchen of Sapper Morton’s home at the beginning of Blade Runner 2049, is difficult to see. And when there are bright moments within a dark portion of the screen — subtitles are a good example — the LG exhibits more blooming than I’ve seen on other RGB LED TVs.
LG MRGB95B specs
Display type: RGB LED
HDR formats: Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG
TV OS: webOS 26
HDMI inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC)
Audio support: Dolby Atmos, Dolby Atmos FlexConnect, Dolby Digital, Auracast
Gaming features: VRR, ALLM, Game Optimizer, G-Sync compatible
Sizes available (inches): 75, 86, 100
The LG 95B can display really vibrant colors thanks to the RGB LED technology. It’s able to cover 100 percent of the P3 color gamut (which is what’s used for films) and nearly 90 percent of the larger BT.2020 color area. But even in Filmmaker mode out of the box, those colors still show visible accuracy issues. Overall, the TV leans toward light blue, so white clouds have a slight blue tint to them and skin tones are cooler than they should be.
After a few days living with the LG MRGB95B, I got used to the slightly blue image (although it was still noticeable). A $3,600 TV in 2026 shouldn’t have the inaccuracies on the MRGB95B.
While the TV performs well in a bright room during the day, when the sun goes down and the lamps turn on, they can wreak havoc on the image. The 95B’s glossy coating is one of the most reflective I’ve seen in a long time. In moderately lit rooms, a lamp or ceiling light directly reflected on the screen causes rainbows to dance across the image. It’s not as bad when the scene is bright, such as the scorching desert of Arrakis in Dune, but once we enter the dark corridors of House Harkonnen, the reflections become incredibly noticeable.
Viewing angles are always a problem for LED TVs — RGB or not — and that’s evident on the LG, too. When only moderately off-axis, the colors become washed out, losing their vibrancy for anyone who’s sitting off to the side.
In a vacuum, the MRGB95B is a good TV for certain situations. It’s really bright and stands up to ambient light well (just avoid having ceiling, wall, or standing lights reflected on the screen), and the colors are vibrant if not totally accurate out of the box. But it doesn’t hold up against other TVs. The Sony Bravia 7 II (which you can find $1,300 cheaper at 75 inches) has better color accuracy and handles reflections better. And the Hisense UR9 performs comparably for less money, too.
But the real competition comes from within LG itself. The LG G6 OLED is only a few hundred dollars more than the MRGB95B, as is the Samsung S95H, and both of those TVs offer significantly better performance with superior color accuracy and viewing angles. The OLEDs don’t get quite as bright, but since they can turn off light at the pixel level, contrast is remarkable...

title_fa: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?

content_en:
At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman unveiled the company’s new AI agent Dots — and told the crowd that the company wants to “set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI.” OpenAI would spend the day taking veiled shots at Meta’s Muse, its primary competitor, for failing to keep users’ data safe. Yet Muse itself, a couple of months earlier, had launched as a supposedly safer alternative to predecessor OpenClaw — with CEO Mark Zuckerberg promising it was “built from the ground up for privacy and security.”
AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?
Meta positioned its Muse agent as a safer alternative to OpenClaw. OpenAI promises Dots is a safer alternative to Muse.
Meta positioned its Muse agent as a safer alternative to OpenClaw. OpenAI promises Dots is a safer alternative to Muse.
In an age when companies hoard customers’ personal data and cyberattacks are a dime a dozen, AI labs are trying to convince users to share even more information with their agents. Their latest strategy for success is one-upping the competition by promising that unlike their rivals, they’ll keep user data away from prying eyes. The question is whether companies can keep these promises.
Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, wrote on X that the company’s “goal with muse was to build something like openclaw that we could make safe and secure and easy to use and scale to billions of people.” User data is stored on a secure VM, what Zuckerberg described as an “isolated linux computer with a browser, CPU, memory, and storage.” The company said that most of the effort in building Muse was related to “careful design and engineering to operate [it] more safely.” Meta’s blog post continued, “Muse can and will still make mistakes, but we expect they’ll be much less frequent and cause much less damage due to the safety systems we’ve built in.”
But though Muse topped the App Store charts and, per Apptopia, gained 600,000 daily active users in the US within weeks, Meta’s promises seem to have fallen short. Although data is isolated from other users, and the company plans to introduce a way “to cryptographically and verifiably prevent Meta from accessing data in your VM” later this year, Meta itself can still access the data. A security researcher quickly exposed a zero-day vulnerability that could allow someone to take control of Muse (which has since been patched), raising fears of outside attacks. Multiple serious security issues reportedly cropped up at the last minute before launch, one of which could have allowed users to access Meta’s own internal databases, per 404 Media.
Muse also appears to liberally collect (and in some cases, hand out) data. It defaults to allowing Meta to train models on what users put into it, though it’s possible to opt out. An Inc. reporter complained that Muse uploaded and read his private messages without him asking it to, and a YouTuber said it had offered his address to a stranger via Marketplace — in both cases, Muse was functioning apparently as intended, but the user didn’t realize how far it would go. The platform creates “detailed profiles of all your friends and family,” as Wired reported. None of this is necessarily unexpected from Meta, but it certainly doesn’t back up the idea that Muse is uniquely privacy- or security-conscious.
OpenAI seized on this fact when announcing Dots in late September. Alexander Embiricos, OpenAI’s Codex product lead, said onstage at DevDay that OpenAI is focused on having the “most trustworthy, safe, and secure assistant,” and CEO Sam Altman demonstrated ways that people could exert control over their individual Dots, such as setting a rule that it should never make a purchase over a certain dollar amount. “I think we’re in a different position to Meta in that they don’t have an AI product that has 1.2 billion users,” said Glen Coates, OpenAI’s head of app platform, adding that “launching something that makes those kinds of mistakes is something that we would try to take the care to avoid.”
Altman himself also pushed the privacy angle at DevDay. To court business customers, executives presented a framework allowing enterprises to have “stronger controls” over their data and zero data retention policy options (meaning no data is stored on OpenAI servers). Indeed, so far, there haven’t been many privacy scandals with Dots — although since it’s only available on the $100-and-up ChatGPT subscription tiers, there are also likely fewer people using it.
People may still not feel comfortable giving OpenAI their personal data, in part simply because AI agents require so much of it. For instance, The Verge’s Allison Johnson felt uncomfortable typing in her bank information when the bot asked as part of a relevant task (Muse has a Stripe integration to take care of that).
Not all companies are making privacy promises, of course. Instinct was publicly criticized for reportedly overly-broad terms of service that gave it unfettered access to data; since then, the company seems to have made adjustments. For now, AI labs seem to be counting on a three-part approach to popularizing AI agent use with the general public: Make them useful, make them cute and disarming to help offset the creepiness, and make promises about privacy — and hope they hold up.

- Decade-old RAM is making a comeback
- GTA VI leaks continue with a lengthy (and very nude) gameplay video
- The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
- Satya Nadella says we should assume all AI models are ‘compromised’
