title_en: Amazon’s new Kindles appear to have a light leak problem
title_fa: Amazon’s new Kindles appear to have a light leak problem
excerpt_en: Some users are reporting that the new Kindles have a light leak issue that is especially apparent when using dark mode. The latest base-model Kindles have a flush bezel that gives them a sleek appearance and looks great… as long as you keep the lights on. But things can change...
excerpt_fa: Some users are reporting that the new Kindles have a light leak issue that is especially apparent when using dark mode. The latest base-model Kindles have a flush bezel that gives them a sleek appearance and looks great… as long as you keep the lights on. But things can change...
content_en:
Some users are reporting that the new Kindles have a light leak issue that is especially apparent when using dark mode. The latest base-model Kindles have a flush bezel that gives them a sleek appearance and looks great… as long as you keep the lights on. But things can change once you turn down the lights and turn up the brightness on the e-reader.
Amazon’s new Kindles appear to have a light leak problem
Reddit users are reporting shadows and visible LEDs around screen edge of new Kindles.
Reddit users are reporting shadows and visible LEDs around screen edge of new Kindles.
In some cases, users see shadows around the edges of the screen, or even visible LED strips. The issue appears to affect both the plastic and aluminum models in all colors. Some minor glowing around the edges might be a byproduct of the combination of front lighting and a flush screen. But Reddit users say images shared there show something more dramatic that appears to be a defect.
Good e-Reader says that Amazon is aware of the issue and has confirmed that a manufacturing issue may have led to defects in the current batch of Kindles. When contacted by The Verge, Amazon spokesperson Katie Condon said, “In certain, highly specific conditions, such as using dark mode at a higher brightness settings in a dark environment, customers may see a subtle glow on the edge of the display on devices with colored bezels. This can be mitigated by adjusting the front light to a lower level.”
Update October 9th, 2026: Added statement from Amazon.

title_en: Intel is reportedly launching new CPUs on old sockets that support DDR4 memory
title_fa: Intel is reportedly launching new CPUs on old sockets that support DDR4 memory
excerpt_en: If you guessed the RAMpocalypse is involved...
excerpt_fa: If you guessed the RAMpocalypse is involved...
content_en:
Intel is reportedly launching new CPUs on old sockets that support DDR4 memory
This is, of course, due to the AI-fueled RAMpocalypse.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Intel is reportedly releasing new CPUs built on LGA 1700 sockets, according to motherboard manufacturer Gigabyte. The LGA 1700 has been around since 2021, which is a really long time in processor land. Why use relatively ancient technology in brand-new processors that are set to release next year? It all comes down to the price of memory, according to a report by PC Gamer.
LGA 1700 sockets offer support for both DDR5 and DDR4 memory, so the running theory is that upcoming refreshes of Raptor Lake and Alder Lake processors will be configurable to use DDR4 RAM. This is likely to accommodate the ongoing AI-fueled RAMpocalypse, in which memory prices have skyrocketed. Simply put, DDR4 RAM is a lot cheaper than DDR5. Folks can pick up a 32GB DDR4 kit for around $210, but a 32GB DDR5 kit costs upwards of $480.
Intel hasn't confirmed this theory, but VP Robert Hallock recently said that Raptor Lake chips would be sticking around for "years to come." He also suggested that DDR4 integration is one of the primary reasons. "LGA 1700 is still a good socket. Lots of people are still interested in DDR4, so we'll keep offering," he said.
This isn't that surprising, given that many of the company's current line of processors can already be configured to use DDR4 memory. DDR4 isn't as fast as DDR5, but the older memory type is still fine for the vast majority of modern PC games. Testing has revealed that DDR5 sticks deliver a 1 to ten percent FPS improvement. However, this largely depends on the resolution the player chooses and the GPU.

title_en: LumenUs helps automate tedious paperwork in times of grief
title_fa: LumenUs helps automate tedious paperwork in times of grief
excerpt_en: "The day your loved one passes away, you also get this honorary badge of a project manager for a project you had no idea about," said founder Sara Tashakorinia.
excerpt_fa: "The day your loved one passes away, you also get this honorary badge of a project manager for a project you had no idea about," said founder Sara Tashakorinia.
content_en:
When Sara Tashakorinia’s husband died in a car accident eight years ago, the last thing she needed was the roughly 570 hours of paperwork it takes, on average, to settle a loved one’s affairs. But for millions of people each year, this is their reality: a crushing loss, followed by a soullessly mundane avalanche of tedious administrative work.
“The day your loved one passes away, you also get this honorary badge of a project manager for a project you had no idea about, trying to navigate something and learn something when you literally have zero information,” Tashakorinia told TechCrunch.
After years of volunteering to help others navigate what she had to learn on her own, it occurred to Tashakorinia that AI might be able to help — not with the complex, messy experience of grieving and healing, but with the least human parts of the process, like finding the right tax forms, filing insurance claims, and shutting down bank accounts.
The result is LumenUs, the grief care platform that Tashakorinia founded last year to relieve grieving families of some of the administrative burden.
“I think going through it, your threshold of pain is so high, and you’re so lost that you don’t really realize, why do people treat you this way? Why was I left with a stack of paperwork, and why was the funeral home charging me a 300% markup on a casket?” Tashakorinia said.
While Tashakorinia hopes LumenUs will eventually support people throughout the lifelong grieving process, the startup will initially focus on people in the immediate aftermath of a death. When people initially join the platform, they go through an onboarding process in which they share information about the nature of their particular situation.
“We are asking very specific questions to understand the legal and financial means, and their state of mind, and this is only to personalize who they are, and then personalizing what happened,” Tashakorinia said.
From there, the platform organizes tasks by urgency, helping users decipher what needs to be done immediately and what can wait. In some cases, this can even help people discover that they’re entitled to money that can help ease the financial burden of death. In fact, billions of dollars in life insurance benefits go unclaimed because people don’t know they’re available.
“We are using AI to automate as much as we can to save time during this process, and give it back to [users],” she said.
Tashakorinia has a background in cybersecurity, which is sure to prove essential for building a product that asks people to share so much sensitive personal and financial information. She is building LumenUs alongside co-founders Sajad Mirzaei, a former engineer at Google and Box, and Larry Keeley, an innovation scientist, professor, and entrepreneur. The team is also consulting with clinicians and social workers while testing the product.
LumenUs, a participant in this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 — the annual showcase of promising early-stage startups at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco — will launch in early access in October.

title_en: What it's like to spend a night in a Pebble Flow EV RV
title_fa: What it's like to spend a night in a Pebble Flow EV RV
excerpt_en: Staying in the tech-infused trailer can kind of feel like being in a spaceship - in a good way.
excerpt_fa: Staying in the tech-infused trailer can kind of feel like being in a spaceship - in a good way.
content_en:
What it's like to spend a night in a Pebble Flow EV RV
Staying in the tech-infused trailer can kind of feel like being in a spaceship — in a good way.
There's something oddly thrilling (and a little terrifying) about steering a 6,000-pound trailer around a parking lot with nothing more than touchscreen controls on an iPad. It's also the perfect encapsulation of what makes the Pebble Flow electric trailer unlike any other RV out there.
With integrated solar panels, electric motors and automated hitching, the tech-forward trailer is meant to simplify many of the complexities and annoyances that often come with RV ownership. That's Pebble's promise, anyway.
I've been intrigued by the Pebble Flow since my colleagues first saw it on the CES showfloor in 2024. The futuristic-looking RV has a sleek, minimalist interior, a dedicated workspace and full bathroom. But like any CES veteran will tell you, a carefully orchestrated demo is about as far from real-world conditions as you can get. So when Pebble gave me the opportunity to spend a day (and night) in one of their trailers at an actual campsite, I was very curious to see if the $159,000 RV would feel as luxe as it seemed.
After spending nearly 24 hours in a Pebble Flow, I can confirm that the RV is indeed an incredibly comfy space to work and sleep in. But I was even more impressed with how much tech the company has infused into it.
My husband and I stayed in a Flow set up with the same layout we've seen previously from Pebble. There's a dinette at the front end, which can convert into a bed, and a queen-sized Murphy bed in the back that doubles as a desk.
I was worried it might feel cramped with two people working in such a compact space, but we both had plenty of room to stretch out. I spent a few hours with my laptop at both the dinette table and the dedicated desk. I liked the extra comfort of the cushioned bench seats in the kitchen area better, but the table was just wobbly enough to be distracting. The dedicated desk is simple but functional. I don't think it's quite wide enough to set up an external monitor comfortably, but I had plenty of room for my laptop, phones, camera and their respective chargers. The desk also has the advantage of being right next to the back window that can fully open up for fresh air and views.
Speaking of the windows, one of the coolest features is that all of the exterior windows are made of electrochromic "smart glass" that can change from clear to frosted with the touch of a button. It's a nice privacy feature, especially if you're in a shared campsite like I was. However, the combination of the interior LED lights and the frosted, light-blocking windows can also give the inside of a Pebble a slightly disorienting feel since you can't easily tell what time of day it is. It wasn't unpleasant, but it felt a bit like being in a bright, if pleasantly lit, spaceship.
Most of the time, though, my time in the Pebble Flow felt less like a trailer and more like a micro-hotel suite. The bathroom is equipped with a flushing toilet and a separate shower stall. It was easily the nicest bathroom setup I've ever used while camping. The shower was small, but heated up quickly and had good water pressure. The only downside was that the water pump was quite loud while using the sink or shower. If you get up in the middle of the night, the *thud thud thud* of the pump will probably wake up anyone else in the space.
Even so, I slept so much better than I expected. The Murphy bed was surprisingly comfortable, and I appreciated that there were outlets easily accessible on both sides of it.
As comfortable as the inside setup was, I was even more impressed with how the Pebble Flow's tech has simplified so many aspects of RV camping and towing. Each trailer comes with its own iPad Mini that functions as the main controller and hub for the vehicle. It's where you adjust the climate control, lights and other functions. It's also a controller for the trailer's automated hitching and remote control features.
The hitch on the Pebble Flow is equipped with a camera that's able to detect the position of the ball on the hitch of a towing vehicle. As long as the tow vehicle is within four feet of the front of the trailer, you can engage what's essentially a self-hitching mode, even if the two vehicles aren't perfectly lined up.
I watched this in action several times; the whole process took about 45 seconds. As someone with no prior RV experience, I can't speak to how this compares to the typical setup, but I can say that I was able to guide the trailer onto the hitch of a Rivian parked a couple feet away without doing anything other than pressing a couple buttons on an iPad. I also used the same iPad to maneuver the unhitched trailer around its parking spot. I only felt comfortable moving it a foot or so in either direction, but I watched Pebble reps use the remote to parallel park it and move it around the mulch-covered ground of the campsite.
One of Pebble's goals is to streamline the more tedious tasks that can be part of camping with an RV. It has an "instacamp" feature that deploys hydraulic lifts to automatically level and stabilize the trailer when you reach your destination.
Besides being able to remotely control your trailer, the in-wheel motors also help with towing. They provide some added power to help save your gas mileage or EV range a bit. Obviously, I wasn't able to simulate an actual roadtrip, but I was able to experience what it's like to tow a Pebble Flow.
I've never hauled anything bigger than a ski rack, so I was a bit nervous to tow a giant trailer around the campground parking lot and onto Highway 1, but it was actually pretty foolproof. While I was driving, another person held the iPad controller for the trailer — the company advises owners to keep the tablet inside the tow vehicle while you're on the move — and turned the motors on and off. It was an incredibly subtle difference, but it felt stable the whole...

title_en: Amazon and others are done keeping data center deals secret. Is it enough to build trust?
title_fa: Amazon and others are done keeping data center deals secret. Is it enough to build trust?
excerpt_en: Amazon says it will stop using NDAs when negotiating data center deals with local governments, following a similar move from Microsoft earlier this year. Secrecy has fueled community backlash against AI infrastructure, with opposition leading to hundreds of proposed and enacted...
excerpt_fa: Amazon says it will stop using NDAs when negotiating data center deals with local governments, following a similar move from Microsoft earlier this year. Secrecy has fueled community backlash against AI infrastructure, with opposition leading to hundreds of proposed and enacted...
content_en:
Amazon says it will stop using NDAs when negotiating data center deals with local governments, following a similar move from Microsoft earlier this year. Secrecy has fueled community backlash against AI infrastructure, with opposition leading to hundreds of proposed and enacted moratoriums from New York to San Francisco. Meanwhile, a wave of startups is betting that consumers will hand AI agents access to their inboxes, files, and credit cards — if they can get websites to let them in.
On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Anthony Ha, Sean O’Kane, and Rebecca Bellan dig into whether ditching NDAs will change how data center deals get done, why trust may be the real product for personal AI startups, plus a couple of deals of the week.

title_en: Danu Robotics’ fight to build a better recycling robot
title_fa: Danu Robotics’ fight to build a better recycling robot
excerpt_en: For six years, Danu founder Amy Ma has been working on a better way to sort recyclable waste.
excerpt_fa: For six years, Danu founder Amy Ma has been working on a better way to sort recyclable waste.
content_en:
For Danu Robotics founder Amy Ma, the eureka moment came after years of working as a software developer at a London bank. It was the kind of high-touch office that’s typical in finance — but despite all the perks, Ma was alarmed to realize that the building’s recycling bins were being emptied into the trash.
“Even though they have tons of money, there’s all these different recycling bins that just end up in the same place,” Ma told TechCrunch.
The more she dug into the problem, the deeper it seemed to go. It wasn’t just her building. The economics of recycling as a whole often boil down to human beings sorting by hand through streams of waste to pull out different kinds of recyclable material.
“I saw the technology and thought, we can do so much better,” Ma remembers.
Now, she’s making good on that promise with six-year-old, Edinburgh, Scotland-based Danu Robotics, which makes a robot designed to sort through recycling more cheaply and quickly. Ma has been working on that idea for six years and is finally bringing her version of the product to market. Her robot, dubbed H.E.R.O., has a few advantages over its competitors. For example, it picks up items with a pincer claw instead of a suction system. But the bigger difference is the business approach: Danu leverages AI to continuously improve the robot’s software.
The approach is already seeing some traction. Danu has letters of interest from two large customers and $500,000 worth of signed contracts. More notably, more than 200 customers are in its sales pipeline, which gives the company a hook into the $20 billion market for recycling sorting across Europe and North America.
On the back of that promise, Dabnu has raised $5 million in late-seed funding to keep the commercial pressure on.
There’s already a robust market for robotic waste-pickers, particularly the suction-based arms offered by competitors like Glacier and RecycleEye. But Ma believes the economics of recycling will make it easy for a new competitor to prove its worth. Because recycling centers make money off the materials they’re able to sort out, there’s an immediate return on investment for a working system. Ma estimates that a working site will earn $485,000 in additional revenue from having the robot on the sorting line, compared with a $160,000 initial investment and $24,000 in maintenance fees each year. That’s significantly cheaper than the competition, and Ma believes the robot will be more efficient, too.
Since those machines are already shipping, Ma’s next goal is to make the robot sturdier, smaller, and more versatile. Once it’s portable enough, it can be used outside dedicated waste facilities, opening up a whole other world of use cases.
“Once it’s smaller, it can be used as a stand-alone recycling solution for events, for shopping centers, hospitals, or airports to recycle their waste at the source,” Ma told TechCrunch, “and that’s the way we can really change how we’re managing our packaging waste.”
Danu Robotics will be participating in Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, October 13-15 at the Moscone Center in San Francisco.

title_en: We can’t help treating AI like it’s human. But should we?
title_fa: We can’t help treating AI like it’s human. But should we?
excerpt_en: "When we are drawn into even the most primitive exchanges with a relational artifact, we believe it cares for us," Dr. Sherry Turkle writes. "And we are wired to care for it in return."
excerpt_fa: "When we are drawn into even the most primitive exchanges with a relational artifact, we believe it cares for us," Dr. Sherry Turkle writes. "And we are wired to care for it in return."
content_en:
In a tan polo shirt, brown leather belt, and round bolo tie, MIT PhD student Wil Norton kind of looks like a park ranger, leading our tour group through a tropical jungle. We’re not actually on safari, though — we’re at MIT’s Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL). But what we’re about to see is even more exotic than a cheetah or a jaguar: a pair of humanoid Unitree robots, each costing about $50,000.
(“They’ll tell you they cost $16,000,” Norton says. “That’s a lie.”)
We usually only see these robots on YouTube when they’re performing a synchronized martial arts routine, or dancing on “America’s Got Talent.” Here, they’re approachable. Even though I know it isn’t sentient, I want to be its friend.
With Norton’s permission, I approach the robot, whose nickname is Gabe. For a moment, I’m not sure how to interact with something that has a LiDAR sensor where its brain should be, but I default to treating it like a person.
“Hello, sir, it’s nice to meet you,” I say, grabbing its gloved, dexterous hand and shaking it.
I think about this interaction later — my instinctive impulse to be friendly to a robot — when I attend Dr. Sherry Turkle‘s “Artificial Intimacy” book launch at MIT Future Fest.
Turkle, who joined the faculty at MIT in 1976, has been researching the relationship between humans and computers perhaps longer than anyone, charting technology’s psychological impact on us from the first home computers to ChatGPT.
“When we are drawn into even the most primitive exchanges with a relational artifact, we believe it cares for us,” Turkle writes in the book. “And we are wired to care for it in return.”
I’m not alone in my tendency to anthropomorphize robots and large language models (LLMs) — as Turkle notes, it seems to be in our nature. One study found that about 70% of people are polite when interacting with AI, while another showed that users are more likely to say “please” or “thank you” to chatbots once a conversation has progressed past a first prompt-and-response.
“People tend to categorize whether this is the right use or wrong use, but I don’t think that is a clear boundary,” Dr. Pat Pataranutaporn, a colleague of Turkle who founded the Cyborg Psychology research group at the MIT Media Lab, told TechCrunch. “The question is, who are we becoming when we talk to [AI]?”
There’s no material consequence of my politeness toward Gabe the robot, but as LLMs infiltrate everything from Google searches to customer service interactions, it has become routine for people to interact with these seemingly sentient chatbots. We’re more vulnerable than ever to the flip side of this impulse, which is that some people can ascribe so much legitimacy to the feelings of chatbots — which are programmed to never spark conflict — that they end up favoring them over other humans.
“You can think of it like fantasy and fiction. We go to the cinema even though we know the story is completely fictional, but we want to experience a certain dimension of human experience that maybe our reality cannot give us,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we benefit from that ability to experience other dimensions of human experience without losing it to the fantasy, where you can no longer come back to the reality?”
Pataranutaporn describes himself as a “critical optimist,” and he studies AI’s potential to contribute to human flourishing. But he’s well aware of how dangerous this technology can be in the extremes. He even served as an expert in a wrongful death lawsuit over the suicide of 14-year-old Sewell Setzer, III, whose mother sued the chatbot platform Character.AI, alleging that a chatbot modeled after a “Game of Thrones” character had encouraged her son to end his life.
“It can create a situation where people don’t feel agency in actually creating their own future — like when you say that AI will replace everyone, people ask, what are we gonna do? And these companies are not really responding ethically or responsibly,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we have imagination while still being responsible for the impact of that imagination?”
While Turkle’s book explores the risk of turning to AI for emotional support, rather than other people, she doesn’t think that AI-human interactions are universally harmful.
She recalls a project she advised in which a student created an AI bot to help people practice for job interviews.
“My big metaphor is, stay in your lane, chatbot!” Turkle said at the event. “Coaching for a job interview? That’s a lane. I can do that … A chatbot that says to a three-year-old, ‘I’m your parent, you can talk to me, not your parents,’ is not in a lane.”
But when this technology deviates from its lane even slightly, we become vulnerable to the way it can slowly chip away at our skepticism and make us trust it. It can start with something as simple as a handshake.

title_en: Tesla renames ‘Full Self-Driving’ to ‘Tesla Assisted Driving’ in Europe
title_fa: Tesla renames ‘Full Self-Driving’ to ‘Tesla Assisted Driving’ in Europe
excerpt_en: The name change is enough for Germany's transport minister to start advocating for Europe-wide adoption of the driver assistance software.
excerpt_fa: The name change is enough for Germany's transport minister to start advocating for Europe-wide adoption of the driver assistance software.
content_en:
Tesla has changed the name of its advanced driver assistance system in Europe after pushback from Germany’s transportation ministry. It’s now called “Tesla Assisted Driving,” instead of “Full Self-Driving (Supervised).”
It’s a big capitulation from Tesla, which has been using the “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” name for years despite the system requiring humans to pay attention to the road and take over when necessary. But the name change could help Tesla achieve its goal of wider adoption on the continent, which could unlock a potentially massive new revenue stream for the company.
Germany’s transport minister, Steffen Bilger, said earlier this month that calling the software “Full Self-Driving” was somewhat misleading because it doesn’t perform the entire task of driving. He spoke with Tesla last month, and the company suggested the name change, according to an official release from the ministry. Bilger said he will now advocate for approval of Tesla Assisted Driving across Europe ahead of an EU-wide vote that could happen later this year. Tesla CEO Elon Musk thanked Bilger on X this week.
Musk has spent years agitating for Full Self-Driving (Supervised), or FSD, to be approved in Europe. “FSD in Europe will save lives of people in the car, as well as vulnerable road users like pedestrians, cyclists, and pets,” he wrote on X in June 2025. “Please let your government know that you want approval.”
In March of this year, he wrote that the “extreme regulatory burden” of the EU “stifles innovation in Europe,” adding that Europe “will love Tesla self-driving!”
Just a few weeks later, the Netherlands became the first European country to approve FSD (Supervised). On Wednesday, Reuters reported that Tesla’s campaign for European approval has been “built on faulty company safety research” and “flawed studies.” The outlet also reported that the Dutch vehicle safety regulator, RDW, faced fierce pressure from Tesla and its legion of online supporters.
Tesla’s software has certainly become more capable over the years. What used to be little more than a mix of lane centering and adaptive cruise control is now a driver assistance system that some owners use for nearly 100% of their daily driving. FSD can pull in and out of parking spots and navigate surface streets and highways. Tesla is so confident in the technology that it recently made it possible for FSD to intervene in a human driver’s control of the vehicle if it senses an oncoming collision — even if FSD is not active.
But FSD has been at the center of federal investigations and civil lawsuits over crashes in which it was allegedly in use. Its less capable predecessor, Autopilot, has been associated with dozens of fatalities. Tesla discontinued Autopilot earlier this year after a judge ruled Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing about the system’s capabilities.

title_en: Remember Orkut? Its founder wants to bring it back
title_fa: Remember Orkut? Its founder wants to bring it back
excerpt_en: Orkut's founder is now taking aim at algorithms and AI-generated content.
excerpt_fa: Orkut's founder is now taking aim at algorithms and AI-generated content.
content_en:
Orkut, the once-popular social networking platform that shut down more than a decade ago, may finally be making a comeback, as its founder has called on users to help revive it with a renewed focus on friendship, community, and human connection.
In a post on X on Thursday, Orkut Büyükkökten, the founder of the eponymous social network, urged users to visit Orkut.com and add their names in support of bringing it back, as well as invite others to join.
Orkut first debuted in 2004 as a side project by Büyükkökten, 51, while he was at Google. The social network went on to become hugely popular in India and Brazil but later lost ground to Facebook. Google eventually shut it down in September 2014, shifting its focus to other platforms, including Google+ and YouTube.
In a letter published on Orkut.com, Büyükkökten criticized how social media has evolved over the past two decades, particularly the growing influence of algorithms and AI-generated content. “Artificial intelligence is extraordinary technology, but it’s dissolving the one premise that made social networking special and worth building: that there was a person on the other side,” he wrote.
“I know how to get there: we rebuild the internet we first loved. The one with authentic people, real connection, and genuine belonging,” Büyükkökten added.
This is not the first time Büyükkökten has explored a return to social networking. In 2016, two years after Orkut’s shutdown, he launched another social network, Hello, focused on connecting people through shared interests. The platform shut down in 2020 after attracting more than 2 million downloads worldwide, compared with Orkut’s about 300 million active users.
In 2022, Büyükkökten hinted at another social networking venture in a note on Orkut.com, saying that he was “building something new.” He did not offer further details. Two years later, he told WIRED he was working on a social network that would “leverage AI and machine learning” to bring people together and build communities. That platform has yet to launch.
Now, Büyükkökten is asking people to register their support for Orkut’s return. He has, however, not clarified whether a new version of the platform is already in development or whether it will ever launch.
An email sent to Orkut seeking comment from Büyükkökten did not elicit a response.

title_en: a16z’s Olivia Moore on the state of consumer AI
title_fa: a16z’s Olivia Moore on the state of consumer AI
excerpt_en: Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges.
excerpt_fa: Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges.
content_en:
I wrote this week about the bleak economics of consumer AI — but where some see a crisis, others see an opportunity.
Olivia Moore covers consumer AI as a partner at Andreessen Horowitz — and on Monday, she released a report on the top 100 consumer AI apps. ChatGPT is still the biggest player by a mile, but smaller players like Suno and ElevenLabs are showing real staying power. Even more interesting is what we don’t see, as Moore’s report details half a dozen consumer categories that seem to be completely untouched by AI.
Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges. On a call this week, I talked with her about the unusual economics of consumer AI and why it’s still early days for the category.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
It’s an interesting moment for a report about consumer AI, since we’ve seen OpenAI pivot back to enterprise this year. It’s inspired a lot of pessimism about the overall revenue picture for consumer AI, including from me. But I take it you’re more optimistic?
I agree with you that OpenAI has moved back towards the enterprise. To me, it’s not necessarily a pivot because they’re still launching a lot in consumer. It’s more of an expansion. But I don’t blame them, as much as I love consumer, because almost all of the AI revenue thus far has come from subscriptions and then token usage. And that is much more concentrated on the enterprise and prosumer side.
How can consumer AI products change that revenue problem? The State of Markets report reminded us that just 2.2% of U.S. households are paying for AI. Do we need that number to rise before the market becomes attractive?
I actually don’t know if I want to see that user number increase. I’m more interested in getting back to a world where the consumer is monetized in a way that isn’t subscription dollars out of their own pocket.
I think it’s very easy in Silicon Valley, with people who are high-income and have corporate cards to pay for those tools, to say, “oh well, I’d rather pay for the product.” But I think most people would actually rather have free access to something and see some ads, and then they can decide if they want to subscribe or not to make the ads go away.
The other challenge is the marginal cost of AI services, which is still a lot higher than classic internet services like Facebook or Google Search. Do you see a lot of these services finding ways to keep those costs down, whether it’s open source or other lightweight models?
Yeah, I think we’re seeing improvements there. Even ChatGPT now has a Go plan, which is just $8 a month, and I’m assuming it runs on cheaper models. We don’t necessarily need frontier intelligence for every task, and so that could mean cheaper models, especially for some consumer use cases. It could also mean more consumer companies building on top of open source models. We’ve heard a lot of that from our founders lately, and it really feels like it’s starting to change.
The problem is that right now, the users driving the revenue are doing coding and other technical automation, where they probably do need frontier intelligence. I think as we get more people building for the consumer, where the model is not the product, we’ll start to see lower-cost models used more often.
It’s unusual to talk about technical automation in a consumer service, which feels like another unique feature of AI. Are we starting to blur the lines between consumer and enterprise?
I wrote an article about this maybe a year or so ago called The Great Expansion trying to get at this. Pre-AI, you would have companies like Canva that were consumer-first and often took six or seven years to even add teams or enterprise plans. Now we’re seeing companies like Gamma, ElevenLabs, and Cursor that start as consumer and within 18 months become majority-enterprise businesses.
Almost all of what we think of as consumer AI, I would argue, is prosumer AI. This really comes out on the revenue list, where there’s basically like three categories that power users are spending on. There’s product-building apps, so like Lovable, Replit, and Fal. There’s product marketing, which is AI ad generators like Higgsfield or HeyGen. Then there’s general work management, like Manus, Fireflies AI, and Granola. Those are like being paid for by consumers to start with, but I would argue that they’re not consumer in the way that we would think about pre-AI.
There are also all these whitespace categories: social apps, dating apps, marketplaces, retail, travel, finance, health. There are no entrants in our top 100 list in those categories, which is pretty surprising. And that’s what I think we need to see over the next six months.
So maybe we haven’t really seen true consumer AI yet?
It’s definitely very early.

I agree with you that OpenAI has moved back towards the enterprise. To me, it’s not necessarily a pivot because they’re still launching a lot in consumer. It’s more of an expansion. But I don’t blame them, as much as I love consumer, because almost all of the AI revenue thus far has come from subscriptions and then token usage. And that is much more concentrated on the enterprise and prosumer side.
How can consumer AI products change that revenue problem? The State of Markets report reminded us that just 2.2% of U.S. households are paying for AI. Do we need that number to rise before the market becomes attractive?
I actually don’t know if I want to see that user number increase. I’m more interested in getting back to a world where the consumer is monetized in a way that isn’t subscription dollars out of their own pocket.
I think it’s very easy in Silicon Valley, with people who are high-income and have corporate cards to pay for those tools, to say, “oh well, I’d rather pay for the product.” But I think most people would actually rather have free access to something and see some ads, and then they can decide if they want to subscribe or not to make the ads go away.
The other challenge is the marginal cost of AI services, which is still a lot higher than classic internet services like Facebook or Google Search. Do you see a lot of these services finding ways to keep those costs down, whether it’s open source or other lightweight models?
Yeah, I think we’re seeing improvements there. Even ChatGPT now has a Go plan, which is just $8 a month, and I’m assuming it runs on cheaper models. We don’t necessarily need frontier intelligence for every task, and so that could mean cheaper models, especially for some consumer use cases. It could also mean more consumer companies building on top of open source models. We’ve heard a lot of that from our founders lately, and it really feels like it’s starting to change.
The problem is that right now, the users driving the revenue are doing coding and other technical automation, where they probably do need frontier intelligence. I think as we get more people building for the consumer, where the model is not the product, we’ll start to see lower-cost models used more often.
It’s unusual to talk about technical automation in a consumer service, which feels like another unique feature of AI. Are we starting to blur the lines between consumer and enterprise?
I wrote an article about this maybe a year or so ago called The Great Expansion trying to get at this. Pre-AI, you would have companies like Canva that were consumer-first and often took six or seven years to even add teams or enterprise plans. Now we’re seeing companies like Gamma, ElevenLabs, and Cursor that start as consumer and within 18 months become majority-enterprise businesses.
Almost all of what we think of as consumer AI, I would argue, is prosumer AI. This really comes out on the revenue list, where there’s basically like three categories that power users are spending on. There’s product-building apps, so like Lovable, Replit, and Fal. There’s product marketing, which is AI ad generators like Higgsfield or HeyGen. Then there’s general work management, like Manus, Fireflies AI, and Granola. Those are like being paid for by consumers to start with, but I would argue that they’re not consumer in the way that we would think about pre-AI.
There are also all these whitespace categories: social apps, dating apps, marketplaces, retail, travel, finance, health. There are no entrants in our top 100 list in those categories, which is pretty surprising. And that’s what I think we need to see over the next six months.
So maybe we haven’t really seen true consumer AI yet?
It’s definitely very early.

title_en: Automattic interim CFO resigns just weeks after boardroom shakeup
title_fa: Automattic interim CFO resigns just weeks after boardroom shakeup
excerpt_en: Automattic's interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left the company less than a month after taking the role, TechCrunch has learned. Sources say his departure followed a demotion back to his previous position, marking another executive exit amid the organization's...
excerpt_fa: Automattic's interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left the company less than a month after taking the role, TechCrunch has learned. Sources say his departure followed a demotion back to his previous position, marking another executive exit amid the organization's...
content_en:
Automattic’s interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left his position after less than a month, TechCrunch has learned. Klaperman had been elevated to the new job last month after the governance crisis at the WordPress.com parent company, which saw its entire board either quit or be fired.
The company confirmed the departure with the following statement, shared by Automattic’s director of communications Megan Fox: “Automattic will always be grateful for Jeremy Klaperman’s leadership. We wish him the best of luck on his next endeavor.”
Before serving as the organization’s interim finance chief, Klaperman had served as the CFO of Automattic’s VIP Enterprise business unit.
He was meant to replace the former CFO, Mark Davies, who had briefly become Automattic’s CFO after the company’s board members voted to put CEO Matt Mullenweg on leave in September. Within 33 hours of the board’s decision, Mullenweg retook the CEO role, and the board was wiped clean.
Automattic’s chief legal officer Andy Missan had also left the company alongside Davies. Both executives had signed reciprocal severance deals during Mullenweg’s short leave of absence, TechCrunch previously reported. Automattic’s new board of directors was announced in late September, and includes best-selling science-fiction author Hugh Howey; two co-founders of the now-defunct social app IRL, Henry Khachatryan and Krutal Desai; plus author Amy Chan.
A source at Automattic told TechCrunch that Klaperman was upset the board was considering external candidates for the CFO role. Though he was announced internally as interim CFO, the board never legally approved his title, the source said. In addition, there was a disagreement with Mullenweg over a work project related to employee performance reviews, which led to Mullenweg’s demotion of Klaperman back to his former position at VIP. Klaperman resigned shortly thereafter.
Automattic’s spokesperson did not comment on the reason for Klaperman’s departure. The company is still performing an external search for a qualified CFO candidate, we understand.
After publication, the company issued a statement via X post, which implies that Klaperman was offended by the board’s search for external CFO candidates.
It read, “At Automattic, we consider it best practice to evaluate external candidates for critical roles alongside internal people stepping up. We are always talking to and recruiting the best talent. Sometimes people are offended or surprised by this and they resign, sometimes it has led to amazing mentoring or advising situations. We won’t comment on any specific person, but as a company we’re always trying to optimize and redefine ourselves to serve our customers better and promote the ideals we aspire to around Open Source, freedom, liberty, autonomy, and hackers.”
When the company originally announced Klaperman’s new role as interim CFO internally on Automattic’s Slack, Mullenweg reiterated that he had “100% confidence” in the company’s cash and financial position.
Updated after publication with more information about Klaperman’s departure.

title_en: Beyond TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: The Side Events, Parties & Networking You Can’t Miss
title_fa: Beyond TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: The Side Events, Parties & Networking You Can’t Miss
excerpt_en: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is just the beginning. From exclusive networking events and startup showcases to happy hours, dinners, and after-hours meetups, discover what’s happening across San Francisco during Disrupt Week, October 10–16. Find your next connection, your next...
excerpt_fa: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is just the beginning. From exclusive networking events and startup showcases to happy hours, dinners, and after-hours meetups, discover what’s happening across San Francisco during Disrupt Week, October 10–16. Find your next connection, your next...
content_en:
TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 brings founders, investors, operators, builders, and technology leaders to San Francisco from October 13-15. But the activity doesn’t stop when the conference floor closes.
Throughout Disrupt Week, startups and organizations from across the global tech ecosystem will host networking events, happy hours, showcases, demos, dinners, and more.
Here’s what’s happening around San Francisco from Saturday, October 10 through Friday, October 16.
Featured
Polish Innovation Evening: From Ideas to Connections — Poland Meets Silicon Valley
Hosted by Polish Investment and Trade Agency (PAIH) and Upper Silesian Fund
Join us aboard the Historic Klamath for an evening connecting Poland’s innovation ecosystem with Silicon Valley during TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. Meet Polish founders, investors, technology leaders, and ecosystem partners for a discussion followed by informal networking on the San Francisco waterfront.
Learn more & RSVP →
Scaling Nordic Fintech Globally
Hosted by Innovation Norway & Royal Norwegian Consulate General in San Francisco
An evening of fintech, global growth, and great conversations, celebrating Aparta’s selection for TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200.
Learn more & RSVP →
Silicon Valley – Pak US Tech Connect 2026
Hosted by Pakistan Software Export Board (PSEB)
Pak-US Tech Connect brings together Pakistani technology companies, U.S. businesses, industry leaders, investors, partners, and ecosystem stakeholders to explore opportunities for business collaboration, technology partnerships, outsourcing, investment, and market expansion.
Learn more & RSVP →
Saturday, October 10
The First Principles Way to Find the Next 10x Opportunity Hiding in Your Product
9:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m.
Hosted by PrincipiumX
Learn how to use first-principles thinking to uncover overlooked customer needs, differentiate your product, strengthen product-market fit, and identify opportunities for significant growth through a real-world case study.
Sunday, October 11
Happy Hour with AI Created Drinks by AI Barmen!
5:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.
Hosted by AI Barmen
Meet AI Barmen, a robotic bartender that creates personalized cocktails and mocktails through an interactive happy hour experience.
EPIC SF Physical AI Demo Night @ Finding Next Move
2:00 p.m. – 5:00 p.m.
Hosted by EPIC Connector Pte. Ltd.
Ten early-stage startups pitch their products and competitive moats to a hand-selected group of venture investors, followed by an open networking after-party.
International Reception at the European Startup Embassy
6:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.
Hosted by Granite Landings LLC
Join an international startup community for an evening of food, drinks, and networking designed to build better business relationships.
Monday, October 12
The Partnership Exchange by onSpark
6:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.
Hosted by onSpark
The Partnership Exchange turns one evening into a live deal floor for founders who know partnerships drive growth. Walk in with your company, walk out with a real hit list. The onSpark team runs Hit List Live on the spot, mapping the exact partners who can move your revenue this year, then matching you with founders in the room who belong on each other’s lists.
Every attendee gets featured in One Golden Nugget, the co-published spotlight series from Disrupt Week.
Serve, Swipe, & Settle: Mixer for SaaS Leaders Scaling into Embedded Payments
5:00 p.m. – 7:00 p.m.
Hosted by NMI
SaaS founders, developers, and technical leaders can compare notes on embedded payments, monetization, and scaling beyond basic payment infrastructure over Ping-Pong, food, and drinks.
The Future of Work Social Mixer + Open Demos: Worktech, Robotics & Agentic AI
5:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.
Hosted by Ontology of Value
Explore work tech, robotics, and agentic AI through startup pitches, hands-on demos, and networking with founders, operators, and investors shaping the future of work.
Long Lead Time: A Hardware Happy Hour
6:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.
Hosted by Syntro
Connect with founders, engineers, and operators building robotics, chips, rockets, and other frontier hardware over drinks and light bites in a casual setting.
Open to Work: The Game Show
7:00 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.
Hosted by Khwajalabs
A live game show turns the job hunt into networking: compete using your real résumé, pitch yourself onstage, and let the audience decide who advances.
Tuesday, October 13
The Irish Shark Tank
5:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.
Hosted by Enterprise Ireland
Meet and mingle with Ireland’s hottest startups. Enterprise Ireland is back at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and will welcome old friends and new faces to The Irish Shark Tank at Ireland House for happy hour. Availability is limited.
SafetyWing Happy Hour at Harrington’s
5:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.
Hosted by SafetyWing
Meet founders and HR leaders over drinks while connecting with SafetyWing and discussing the challenges of navigating health benefits for startups and their teams.
SF Exclusive VIP Drinks for AI Founders and Accredited Investors
5:30 p.m. – 7:30 p.m.
Hosted by EQUITY X INVESTMENTS, LLC
An invite-only gathering for AI founders and accredited investors featuring drinks, direct introductions, and informal conversations with no pitches or panels.
Harvard Griffin GSAS Alumni Networking Mixer
5:30 p.m. – 7:30 p.m.
Hosted by Harvard Kenneth C. Griffin Graduate School of Arts and Sciences
Connect with Harvard Griffin GSAS alumni living and working in the Bay Area during an informal networking reception. Guests are welcome.
South Asian Investor Founder Connect: TechCrunch Disrupt
5:30 p.m. – 7:30 p.m.
Hosted by American South Asian Network
Connect with South Asian founders, investors, operators, creators, and technology leaders through curated introductions and informal networking.
Real World AI: Connect, Invest & Scale in Taiwan
5:30 p.m. – 6:30 p.m.
Hosted by Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs
Discover how Taiwan, a powerhouse behind the global AI revolution, is bringing AI into the real world through robotics, intelligent hardware,...

title_en: Surveillance company Flock cuts staff as privacy backlash grows
title_fa: Surveillance company Flock cuts staff as privacy backlash grows
excerpt_en: Flock would not say if CEO Garrett Langley would take a pay cut following the reduction in workforce.
excerpt_fa: Flock would not say if CEO Garrett Langley would take a pay cut following the reduction in workforce.
content_en:
Surveillance camera maker Flock is cutting its workforce as the company faces ongoing and growing backlash to its license plate readers and people-tracking technology.
News of the staff cuts comes from Reuters, which reported that Flock is reducing its staff by 18%, or around 270 employees, across the board. The publication said the employees are leaving at the end of October following a voluntary buyout program.
Wired reported last month that Flock was asking some of its employees to leave, citing the need to shrink its staff to avoid mandatory layoffs.
Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel told TechCrunch in a statement on Friday: “Flock recently offered current employees a generous Voluntary Separation Program as part of our efforts to position the company for its next phase of growth. This was a voluntary program, not a layoff, and reflects our continued focus on building a strong, sustainable business for the future.”
Flock’s spokesperson would not comment further when asked by TechCrunch if chief executive Garrett Langley or other executives took a pay cut as part of the program.
Flock has faced heavy criticism and mounting pushback from communities across the United States and legislators looking to rein in the company’s privately run mass surveillance program. Flock has installed over 100,000 license plate-reading cameras across the U.S., which allow police and federal agents to track the location and whereabouts of vehicles passing by them. Dozens of police officers have been arrested, fired, or forced to resign for abusing access to Flock’s system to search, track, and stalk people without a warrant or their permission.
While some cities have moved to take down Flock’s cameras citing public outcry, Flock quickly replaced them, prompting some Americans to destroy the cameras.
Flock has also been criticized for its poor cybersecurity, including allowing cameras to be publicly exposed and accessible from the web. Security experts have questioned Flock’s accuracy after the system has misidentified license plates, resulting in improper police stops and arrests, including a journalist who was driving an authorized review vehicle.
Several law enforcement departments, including Los Angeles’ police department, have allowed their contracts to expire or lapse, citing privacy and civil liberties concerns.

Several law enforcement departments, including Los Angeles’ police department, have allowed their contracts to expire or lapse, citing privacy and civil liberties concerns.

title_en: Webb telescope detects galaxy origin of the farthest fast radio burst we've seen to date
title_fa: Webb telescope detects galaxy origin of the farthest fast radio burst we've seen to date
excerpt_en: Astronomers used the Webb telescope to see where the farthest fast radio burst we've ever seen had come from.
excerpt_fa: Astronomers used the Webb telescope to see where the farthest fast radio burst we've ever seen had come from.
content_en:
Webb telescope detects galaxy origin of the farthest fast radio burst we've seen to date
And the data it provided sheds light on the origins of fast radio bursts.
Back in 2024, scientists detected the farthest fast radio burst we've ever seen to date, thanks to observations by the MeerKAT ground telescope array. Fast radio bursts are ultra-fast radio waves from deep space, which last a fraction of a second but release as much as energy as what the sun emits in three days. They were first discovered in 2007, and not much is known about them. Now, astronomers have used the James Webb telescope to pinpoint the origin of the burst detected in 2024, and it could shed light on the phenomenon's origins.
Webb's near-infrared instruments detected a galaxy in the right location from where the burst had come. Based on measurements from the way its light stretches, the fast radio burst occurred just 3 billion years after the Big Bang. Its origin galaxy existed way back when star formation was at its peak in the universe. In addition, the galaxy that produced it is also 1,000 times smaller than expected. The previous fast radio bursts we've detected took place billions of years later in massive, star-forming galaxies.
There are a couple of theories on how fast radio bursts are produced. One proposes that they're generated by the merger of two neutron stars. But it takes billions of years before two neutron stars — the collapsed cores of massive supergiant stars — collide, which means that bursts can only come from older galaxies.
Another theory suggests that the bursts can come from massive stars exploding in a supernova and leaving behind magnetars, which are rare type of neutron stars that have highly powerful magnetic fields. "Our work suggests that it's very unlikely that this [fast radio burst] was produced by a merger," said Manisha Caleb from the University of Sydney, Australia, who served as lead author on the study published in Science. In other words, their work shows that the origin of this burst was likely a supernova, providing support for the theory that fast radio bursts can come from a certain type of star explosion.

title_en: Xona’s commercial GPS alternative is about to go live
title_fa: Xona’s commercial GPS alternative is about to go live
excerpt_en: Xona's precision timing and navigation service will enter beta testing after SpaceX launches six satellites designed by the company.
excerpt_fa: Xona's precision timing and navigation service will enter beta testing after SpaceX launches six satellites designed by the company.
content_en:
The first precision commercial alternative to GPS is preparing to go live when six satellites designed by the startup Xona Space Systems launch into orbit this month.
A service that competes with free signals provided by governments around the world may seem foolhardy, but Xona is hoping to add navigation and timing to the list of de facto government space monopolies disrupted by venture-backed startups.
Xona was founded in 2019 by a team of five engineers who originally met at Stanford University’s aerospace engineering graduate program. One, Tyler Reid, went on to earn a PhD, writing his thesis on the possibilities of using satellites in low-earth orbit to improve navigation.
GPS and analog satellite networks built by Europe, China, and Russia provide huge value, but are also easy to jam and aren’t precise enough to be used alone for applications like farming robots or self-driving cars. Over “pizza and beer chats,” the friends mulled whether fixing those problems could be a business.
“My knee jerk was like, this is dumb,” Xona CEO Brian Manning told TechCrunch during a recent visit to the company’s headquarters. “Why would anybody replace GPS? It’s free, right? And I started digging into it. People think of GPS as a free service, but the market isn’t the service. The market’s the hardware, and you have billions of devices being sold every year; those things aren’t being given away for free. There’s an immense market that is desperately looking for better performance.”
That didn’t mean the road to delivering such a service was simple. Improving GPS with a stronger signal that offers more precise timing and location data remained a technical challenge. The company needed to develop a unique architecture that would allow its satellites to keep time without expensive atomic clocks onboard, taking advantage of the spacecraft’s proximity to Earth and close communication with ground-based sources of truth.
The other technical challenge the company solved was making sure its signals could be received by existing GPS receivers with a relatively simple software modification. That gives Xona immediate access to the market and smoothes the way through the regulations for broadcasting navigation signals.
Later this month, a SpaceX rocket is scheduled to launch six satellites for Xona. Four are similar to a prototype the company launched last year that proved its technology; those satellites are built around a satellite platform from Aerospace Labs. The other two satellites were built entirely by Xona at its Burlingame, California, headquarters, and are intended to be the foundation of the company’s 258-satellite operational constellation, called Pulsar.
Pulsar will offer centimeter-level precision for geolocation, instead of the meter-level precision provided by GPS, and its signal is strong enough to be detected inside buildings and in urban environments. Manning also believes its signal is powerful enough to deter would-be jammers and spoofers, too.
Xona can begin beta-testing Pulsar with real customers once its satellites are in orbit and passing overhead the mid-latitudes about eight times a day.
Ian Gough, the CEO of TimeBeat, a company that specializes in electronic timing, says the initial pilot will allow his engineers to check and correct the timing provided by its devices around the world. By 2028, Xona hopes to offer full coverage in the U.S., Europe, Japan, and South Korea.
Xona has raised just over $300 million from venture investors since its founding, including $20 million from the U.S. Space Force. While the company is focused on offering a commercial service, the U.S. government is clearly interested in the technology, as jamming and spoofing of satellite navigation services become increasingly common in conflicts.
While there are literally billions of potential users for a new precision timing signal, Xona is also looking ahead to a world of growing autonomy. Reid, whose thesis inspired the company and who now serves as its CTO, worked on self-driving cars at Ford and saw that a service like Pulsar would be needed to realize the potential of autonomous vehicles of all stripes.
Xona’s headquarters boasts an incredible view of planes landing at San Francisco International Airport. Watching the jets come in, Manning points out that among “all the forms of mass transportation, the gold standard for safety is civil aviation. We see Xona and what we’re building being able to play a big part in that … to provide the service to a car, so you can feel as safe taking your hands off the wheel as you are laying back in an airliner.”

title_en: What to expect at Apple's 'Welcome home' event next week
title_fa: What to expect at Apple's 'Welcome home' event next week
excerpt_en: The company is reportedly rebooting its smart home ambitions with a smart display and a whole bunch of other accessories.
excerpt_fa: The company is reportedly rebooting its smart home ambitions with a smart display and a whole bunch of other accessories.
content_en:
What to expect at Apple's 'Welcome home' event next week
The company is reportedly rebooting its smart home ambitions with a smart display and a whole bunch of other accessories.
Apple is hosting its second fall event on October 13, and the "Welcome home" tagline on its invitation heavily suggests it will be focused on smart home products. Depending on your perspective, you could trace the company's entry into the space with the introduction of the Apple TV, HomeKit or the first HomePod, but this new push is reportedly built around the improved functionality of Siri AI and several new pieces of hardware that will run it.
The star of that new hardware lineup will reportedly be the company's first smart display, but it's also expected to introduce updates to the Apple TV and HomePod mini alongside it, too, and possibly a whole lot more. Here's the full rundown of new products Apple could announce at its smart home event.
An Apple smart display or 'HomePad'
All recent reporting indicates Apple is ready to launch its first smart display, a device that marries the audio and AI assistant capabilities of a HomePod with a display that can showcase photos, run apps and act as a dedicated FaceTime device.
Bloomberg reports Apple's so-called "HomePad" will feature a 6-inch square display that will be available attached to a round, HomePod mini-style speaker or a smaller audio set-up that can be mounted alongside the display on a wall. The primary method for interacting with the HomePad is Siri AI, but the device's new tvOS-based "homeOS" will also support touchscreen interactions and include some of the customizable interface elements of the Apple Watch and the iPhone's StandBy mode. The smart display will also be able to run iPadOS-style apps, according to Bloomberg, which opens up the possibility for video streaming and other functionality if developers decide to support it.
Besides acting as a showcase for Siri AI's ability to interact with Apple's HomeKit platform, Apple reportedly also plans for the device to be able to detect who's looking at it and adjust its interface and apps accordingly, though it apparently won't rely on Apple's Face ID technology from the iPhone to make that happen. The feature could let the HomePad switch which calendar or notifications it displays depending on who's looking at the screen — personalization features few other Apple devices offer.
Updates to the HomePod mini and Apple TV
Apple limits access to Siri AI based on a device's A-series or M-series chip, so it makes sense the aging chips in the current HomePod mini (an S5 chip from the Apple Watch Series 5) and the Apple TV 4K (an A15 Bionic chip from the iPhone 13) would need to be swapped out for something new. Bloomberg reports that both the Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini will be updated with faster chips that can run Siri AI, along with modest design updates.
The new Apple TV 4K will reportedly be powered by at least an A19 chip from the iPhone 17 lineup and feature a slightly redesigned remote along. The HomePod mini will come in new colors including green, pink, blue, black and white, according to MacRumors, and will likely feature a chip from a recent Apple Watch so it can handle Siri AI prompts. Apple is also reportedly working on supporting surround sound setups with HomePods, an expansion of the stereo HomePod setups it currently offers through the Apple TV.
Third-party doorbells, locks and cameras
Previous reports suggested Apple was working on its own privacy-focused cameras as part of its smart home lineup, but now Bloomberg reports they might not be sold under Apple's name. The company is reportedly collaborating with LG Electronics to create a series of smart locks, doorbells, thermostats and temperature sensors. The devices will work with Apple's smart home ecosystem but will apparently be manufactured, sold and supported by LG. A later leak suggested similar third-party devices will also come from Schneider Electric, which is apparently making a thermostat for the launch.
The "second-party" partnership includes accessories from Schneider:
• Schneider Home Smart Thermostat
• Schneider Electric Temperature/Humidity SensorOnly the Thermostat shows (placeholder) setup assets. Its setup configuration mentions Proximity Settings.
In total, iOS... https://t.co/8w4fUQ4WpK
— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 7, 2026
This doesn't necessarily preclude Apple from releasing its own versions of these devices down the line, but it does suggest that Apple won't make the first accessories designed for this new era of HomeKit. Considering the threat the company's scale and reach poses to other smart home product makers, it's probably the right move to play nice.

title_en: Anthropic now offers a free vulnerability-finding service for open-source software
title_fa: Anthropic now offers a free vulnerability-finding service for open-source software
excerpt_en: Anthropic is offering open-source projects a new way to check for vulnerabilities with its OSS Scanner.
excerpt_fa: Anthropic is offering open-source projects a new way to check for vulnerabilities with its OSS Scanner.
content_en:
Anthropic now offers a free vulnerability-finding service for open-source software
'Projects that join will receive thorough, periodic security scans by our strongest models at no cost.'
Anthropic is offering open-source projects a new way to check for vulnerabilities with its OSS Scanner. "Projects that join will receive thorough, periodic security scans by our strongest models at no cost," the company announced.
As they've shown recently, AI models are excellent at finding (and exploiting) vulnerabilities. The new scanner could give open-source coders early alerts about potential security issues for free, albeit with the tradeoff that reports won't be reviewed by humans.
"The outputs of this opt-in vulnerability scanner will be fully model-generated, without human review or triage," Anthropic explained. "This will enable faster and more frequent scanning, but means that it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid. These reports will be generated by our strongest models (including Claude Mythos) to give open-source projects the largest defensive advantage."
As Anthropic mentions, it was inspired by OSS-Fuzz open-source software scanner created by Google and the OpenSSF (Open Source Security Foundation) that has been available since 2016. Anthropic already has a paid product called Claude Security that can perform general-access code scanning and patching, but OSS Scanner performs similar security audits at no cost.
Google and Anthropic aren't necessarily providing these products out of altruism. Both companies rely heavily on open-source code projects that underpin the internet, often run by unpaid workers. Security vulnerabilities in such code are highly dangerous, with a recent example of that being the XZ Utils backdoor that could have handed hackers administrative control over millions of systems around the world.

title_en: Netflix releases trailer for its miniseries about Sam Bankman-Fried's scandal-ridden crypto exchange
title_fa: Netflix releases trailer for its miniseries about Sam Bankman-Fried's scandal-ridden crypto exchange
excerpt_en: Watch the trailer for Netflix's The Altruists, a mini-series about the rise and fall of cryptocurrency exchange FTX.
excerpt_fa: Watch the trailer for Netflix's The Altruists, a mini-series about the rise and fall of cryptocurrency exchange FTX.
content_en:
Netflix releases trailer for its miniseries about Sam Bankman-Fried's scandal-ridden crypto exchange
The Altruists, covering the rise and fall of FTX, will start streaming on November 19.
On November 19, Netflix will start streaming The Altruists, an eight-episode mini-series based on the rise and fall of cryptocurrency exchange FTX. The streaming service has released a trailer for the show, featuring its stars Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried and Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison. In the trailer, you'll see how the two of them had met and of the times Ellison's "all in" mentality had supposedly influenced how they ran their business.
Bankman-Fried founded FTX, which offered crypto exchange and crypto hedge fund services, with Gary Wang. FTX originally formed inside Alameda Research, a trading firm co-founded by Bankman-Fried and Ellison, who eventually entered a romantic relationship with each other. They reportedly bonded over "effective altruism" and believed that high-income jobs are worth taking if the end goal is to give income away to charities.
FTX was once one of the world's largest cryptocurrency changes with a daily trading volume of $10 billion until its rapid collapse in 2022. The price of its native token took a nosedive and a lot of users withdrew their money, fearing a liquidity crisis. That led to the revelation that $8 billion of its customers' money had gone missing. In court, Ellison testified that Bankman-Fried directed her to use FTX customer funds to buy property, make political donations and fund Alameda Research. Bankman-Fried was found guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy in late 2023 and was sentenced to 25 years in prison. He recently tried to appeal his fraud conviction, but an appeals court had denied it.

title_en: Meta bans TikTok ads from its platforms in tit-for-tat row
title_fa: Meta bans TikTok ads from its platforms in tit-for-tat row
excerpt_en: Meta has placed a complete ban on ads and marketing from TikTok's US minority owner, ByteDance.
excerpt_fa: Meta has placed a complete ban on ads and marketing from TikTok's US minority owner, ByteDance.
content_en:
Meta bans TikTok ads from its platforms in tit-for-tat row
It called the move 'a normal business practice.'
Meta confirmed that it has banned ads from rival platform TikTok, saying that "declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice," Bloomberg reported. The news follows TikTok's own ban of Instagram and Facebook profile links and Meta ads pressuring TikTok and other social media sites to follow its lead with safety features for minors.
On Thursday, Meta placed a complete ban on ads and marketing from TikTok's US minority owner, China's ByteDance. The ban is in effect in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, the company said. It also applies to third-party advertisers running TikTok-linked campaigns in those countries. "We don't have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps," Meta spokesperson Chris Sgro told Bloomberg.
In August, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement with US states that also forced it to implement child safety features on Facebook and Instagram. Legal experts said that could pressure the company's competitors, particularly TikTok and YouTube, to reshape their apps as well. This summer, the European regulators wrote that TikTok hasn't done enough to ensure minors' safety and that it could impose a fine of up to six percent of the platform's annual revenue.
That puts TikTok and YouTube on the back foot, with both government regulators and Meta itself pressuring them to follow Meta's child safety lead. Meta recently placed ads in major newspapers demanding similar moves from its rivals, while calling out TikTok for failing to show at several US government meetings around screen time and child safety. TikTok, now owned by a consortium of US and UAE investors (including Larry Ellison's Oracle), has so far said very little on the issue.

TikTok, now owned by a consortium of US and UAE investors (including Larry Ellison's Oracle), has so far said very little on the issue.

title_en: SpaceX wants to become a 'major mobile carrier' with low-band spectrum acquisition
title_fa: SpaceX wants to become a 'major mobile carrier' with low-band spectrum acquisition
excerpt_en: SpaceX has revealed its plans to become a major mobile carrier.
excerpt_fa: SpaceX has revealed its plans to become a major mobile carrier.
content_en:
SpaceX wants to become a 'major mobile carrier' with low-band spectrum acquisition
That will allow Starlink’s signal to penetrate walls and reach customers inside buildings.
SpaceX has revealed that it plans to become a major mobile carrier and not just a satellite internet broadband service provider with Starlink. To achieve that goal, it has agreed to acquire 100 percent of Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio. SpaceX says the acquisition is for a "low-band spectrum license portfolio of up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band," though it's still pending FCC approval. Access to the low-band spectrum will address one of the key "technical gaps" remaining to be able to turn Starlink into a major mobile carrier in the US, SpaceX adds.
The company acquired spectrum licenses from EchoStar late last year, including frequencies used in the US for commercial wireless services like mobile and satellite communications. But this particular low-broadband spectrum acquisition will enable Starlink Mobile's signal to penetrate walls and other obstacles. While more established carriers have access to a wider range of bands, this will allow the company to offer a robust and veritable alternative to their offerings. Most mobile devices already support the band, so SpaceX will be able to offer its services to millions of potential customers regardless of their phones.
"With this new low-band spectrum and our Gen2 constellation, Starlink Mobile can now become the first network operator to deploy both satellite and terrestrial spectrum," SpaceX's announcement reads. This new acquisition will allow SpaceX to offer a reliable service indoors, while Starlink's broadband internet will provide customers with a signal even in far-flung places.
The FCC has recently authorized SpaceX to deploy 15,000 Starlink Mobile Gen2 satellites optimized for the 2 GHz spectrum. According to the company, those satellites will be able to deliver more than 100 times the bandwidth of its current satellite generation, giving SpaceX the capability to offer high-speed internet in more regions around the world.

title_en: Fired OpenAI safety researchers dispute their dismissals in open letter
title_fa: Fired OpenAI safety researchers dispute their dismissals in open letter
excerpt_en: Three OpenAI researchers said their firings may have a 'chilling' effect on employees.
excerpt_fa: Three OpenAI researchers said their firings may have a 'chilling' effect on employees.
content_en:
Fired OpenAI safety researchers dispute their dismissals in open letter
They said company communications around the firing may have made colleagues 'afraid to speak.'
Three OpenAI safety researchers have posted an open letter to OpenAI disputing their dismissals. Jasmine Wang, Mikita Balesni and Tomek Korbak wrote that the "very public manner" of the company's communications around the firings could have a "chilling" effect on employees at a time when "the world's safety depends on them."
Last week, OpenAI dismissed three employees who allegedly shared information with an external AI safety organization. The company said in a statement that the employees "violat[ed] our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information... breaking the trust essential to our work." In the face of recent serious and potentially illegal OpenAI agent hacks of Hugging Face and other organizations, though, the firing of safety employees raised awkward questions and caught the attention of lawmakers.
"We have become concerned that internal and external communications around our firing have
made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an
integral part of working at OpenAI," the joint letter from the dismissed employees states. "We could raise safety concerns and disagree openly [before], and were encouraged to draw on the expertise of independent safety organizations. This is part of what made OpenAI special, and why we are immensely proud to have been part of the team."
The researchers stated that they "acted in line with OpenAI's mission and within the working norms of the time," and that the firing "leaves us worried that the norms inside OpenAI are shifting and that employees are now unclear on where they stand."
Addressing other rumors, Wang, Belsni and Korbak also said they were not the leak source for a The Information article involving OpenAI's new, less monitorable architectures and don't believe they engaged with external parties outside their mandate. They added that communication with external parties was done "in coordination and discussion with board members and the C-suite," and that Wang notified an executive when she accidentally clicked on a sensitive email.
In parting, the former employees made several recommendations to OpenAI. They said that the company should adhere to its public commitments to embed third-party safety auditors and not use their firing as a "pretext for stepping away from those partnerships." They added that OpenAI must preserve the monitorability of frontier models and maintain an "open and transparent culture of dialogue between its safety researchers and the rest of the safety ecosystem."
In a thread on X, Jasmine Wang wrote that OpenAI leadership "is saying that they strongly agree with our letter," while expressing concern about OpenAI's, well, openness. "We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances," she wrote. "Unless employees take a stand now against this kind of maneuver, I am concerned we will not be the last. The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why."
